rsi.label: Relative Strength Index
rsi.oneLiner: A 0–100 speedometer for price movement — how hard the stock has been rising or falling recently.
rsi.what: RSI measures how strongly a stock has been moving over roughly the last two weeks, on a scale of 0 to 100. Think of it as a speedometer: it does not tell you the direction of the road (that is the trend), only how fast the price is travelling and whether that pace is sustainable. Above 70 is 'overbought' — like an engine at redline; below 30 is 'oversold' — a car braking hard.
rsi.howCalculated: Compares the average size of recent up-days to down-days over 14 periods, squeezed into a 0–100 range.

bands.text: ${value} — extreme overbought. In strong trends this can persist, but risk/reward for new entries is poor.
${value} — overbought territory. The stock has risen fast; pullback risk is elevated but this alone is NOT a sell signal in a strong trend.
${value} — the sweet spot: upward momentum without being stretched.
${value} — downward pressure, but not yet at extreme oversold levels.
${value} — oversold. A bounce may be near, OR something fundamental is wrong. Check the news before treating it as a bargain.

rsi.whyMatters: RSI helps answer: 'Is this move running out of steam, or still has room?' It times entries better than it predicts reversals.
rsi.scoringImpact: In our engine: RSI 50–70 adds positive points; extreme overbought (>85) without fundamental support can trigger a dealbreaker flag; oversold is judged by surrounding context, not mechanically.
commonMistakes: Selling just because RSI is overbought — in strong uptrends stocks can stay above 70 for weeks while making huge gains.
Buying just because RSI is oversold — a stock can stay oversold while a company deteriorates.
Using RSI alone instead of combining with trend (MA alignment) and volume confirmation.
rsi.example: NVDA at RSI 72 during a product-launch rally stayed overbought for three weeks and gained another 18% — overbought marked STRENGTH there. The same reading on a stock with falling revenue preceded a 25% drop.

ma_alignment.label: MA Alignment
ma_alignment.oneLiner: Checks whether the 20-, 50-, and 200-day moving averages are stacked in order — like confirming all traffic lights are green.
ma_alignment.what: Moving averages smooth out daily price noise to reveal the underlying trend. We look at three timeframes: 20 days (short-term), 50 days (medium-term), and 200 days (long-term). Alignment means they are stacked in the same direction — like a set of traffic lights all showing green for an uptrend or red for a downtrend.
ma_alignment.howCalculated: Compares the relative positions of SMA20, SMA50, and SMA200. If SMA20 > SMA50 > SMA200 it is bullish; if SMA20 < SMA50 < SMA200 it is bearish; anything else is mixed.

bands.text: BULLISH — short-term > mid-term > long-term. All three trends agree: the stock is in a clear uptrend.
BEARISH — short-term < mid-term < long-term. All three trends agree: the stock is in a clear downtrend.
MIXED — no clear order among the three averages. The stock lacks a strong directional trend right now.

ma_alignment.whyMatters: A stock with aligned moving averages is like a car with all passengers agreeing on the destination — the ride is smoother. Mixed alignment means conflicting signals, making entries riskier.
ma_alignment.scoringImpact: This is one of the heaviest-weighted factors. Bullish alignment contributes a large positive boost. Bearish alignment pushes the score negative. Mixed adds nothing.
commonMistakes: Treating mixed alignment as a signal — it is the absence of a signal, not a third trend direction.
Ignoring alignment and chasing a stock that is above its 20-day MA but below its 200-day MA.
ma_alignment.example: AAPL shows SMA20 at $175, SMA50 at $170, SMA200 at $160 — all stacked upward. This bullish alignment added +0.4 to the technical score and helped confirm the uptrend before a 12% rally.

adx.label: ADX (Average Directional Index)
adx.oneLiner: A volume knob for trend strength — higher ADX means the trend has more conviction behind it, regardless of direction.
adx.what: ADX measures how strong a trend is, not which way it goes. Think of it as a volume knob: the higher the number, the more 'volume' or conviction behind the move. A reading above 25 means a trend is in place; above 50 means it is very strong; below 20 means the market is choppy or range-bound.
adx.howCalculated: Derived from the smoothed difference between the positive and negative directional indicators (+DI and -DI) over 14 periods. The result is a 0–100 scale where higher equals stronger trend.

bands.text: ${value} — very strong trend. Big moves are happening with high conviction.
${value} — trending market with decent strength. A trend exists and has some power behind it.
${value} — weak or choppy price action. No clear trend; trend-following strategies are less effective here.

adx.whyMatters: A stock can be going up, but if ADX is low, the move might be weak and easily reversed. High ADX gives confidence that the trend will continue — like a strong current in a river versus a stagnant pond.
adx.scoringImpact: Strong trends (ADX >= 25) boost the technical score. Very strong trends (ADX >= 50) add more. Weak trends (ADX < 20) are neutral. Extreme ADX with poor positioning can signal an exhausted trend.
commonMistakes: Assuming high ADX means 'buy' — it only means the trend is strong, not that the direction favors you.
Ignoring ADX and trading crossovers in choppy markets (ADX < 20) where whipsaws are frequent.
adx.example: TSLA during its 2020 run had ADX above 40 for months — the trend was powerful. In summer 2022, ADX dropped below 15 while price drifted sideways — traders using trend-following lost money on false breakouts.

atr_pct.label: ATR % (Average True Range Percent)
atr_pct.oneLiner: The stock's typical daily move as a percentage of price — your guide for how wide to set stop losses and how many shares to buy.
atr_pct.what: ATR measures how much a stock typically moves each day (its volatility). We express it as a percentage of price so you can compare a $10 stock to a $500 stock. A 5% ATR means the stock swings ~$5 on a $100 stock or ~$25 on a $500 stock — same percentage, very different dollar moves.
atr_pct.howCalculated: Average True Range over 14 periods divided by current price, multiplied by 100. True Range captures the full daily move including gaps.

bands.text: ${value}% — HIGH volatility. This stock moves a lot each day. Bigger potential gains, but also bigger potential losses. Use wider stops and smaller positions.
${value}% — moderate volatility. Normal stock movement with occasional bigger days. Standard stop-loss sizing works well.
${value}% — low volatility. This stock is steady and predictable. Smaller day-to-day moves mean tighter stops and potentially larger positions.

atr_pct.whyMatters: Volatility tells you how bumpy the ride will be. High volatility stocks need wider stop losses and smaller position sizes — like driving a monster truck versus a sedan. Low volatility stocks are calmer but may have less profit potential.
atr_pct.scoringImpact: Used to calculate suggested stop loss and position size. Extreme volatility (>5%) is flagged as a dealbreaker. Normal volatility (2–5%) is ideal.
commonMistakes: Using the same stop-loss percentage on a 1% ATR stock and a 6% ATR stock — the latter will stop you out on normal noise.
Confusing ATR% with beta — ATR% is the stock's own daily range; beta is how it moves relative to the market.
atr_pct.example: NVDA at $400 with ATR% of 3.5% means a typical day sees a $14 swing. A 2 ATR stop would be $28 (7%). If you risk 1% of a $50K account ($500), you'd buy ~18 shares. Same math on a 1% ATR stock would buy ~60 shares.

volume_ratio.label: Volume Ratio (Relative Volume)
volume_ratio.oneLiner: Today's volume compared to the 10-day average — tells you if big money is paying attention right now.
volume_ratio.what: Compares today's trading volume to the average volume over the last 10 days. A ratio of 2.0 means today's volume is double the norm. You may see this called 'Relative Volume' (rvol) elsewhere — it is the same number. High volume confirms a price move is real; low volume suggests it might be a head fake.
volume_ratio.howCalculated: Current day's volume divided by the 10-day average volume. A ratio of 1.0 is exactly average; 3.0 is three times average.

bands.text: ${value}x — EXTREME volume. Something major is happening. Big institutions are aggressively buying or selling.
${value}x — above-average volume. More interest than usual, confirming the current price move.
${value}x — normal volume. Typical trading activity; no unusual conviction.
${value}x — below-average volume. Less interest than usual. Moves on low volume can be unreliable.

volume_ratio.whyMatters: High volume confirms that a price move is real. A stock going up on high volume = genuine buying pressure. A stock going up on low volume = might be a false move. Volume is the 'lie detector' for price action.
volume_ratio.scoringImpact: High volume (>1.5x) adds positive points when direction aligns with the trend. Low volume doesn't hurt but doesn't help either. The screener's volume badge (e.g., '×2.3') uses this same value.
commonMistakes: Getting excited by high volume on a down day — heavy selling volume is bearish, not bullish.
Ignoring low volume breakouts — a stock breaking resistance on 0.5x volume often fails.
volume_ratio.example: META earnings day: volume ratio 4.2x. The stock gapped up 15% on massive volume — institutions were aggressively accumulating. Two weeks later, a 5% rally on 0.6x volume quickly reversed — no conviction behind it.

bb_position.label: Bollinger Band Position
bb_position.oneLiner: Where the price sits inside its volatility channel — inside is normal, outside means something unusual is happening.
bb_position.what: Bollinger Bands create a 'price channel' around the 20-day moving average. The bands widen when volatility increases and narrow when it decreases. This metric tells you whether the price is inside the channel (normal), above the upper band (strong momentum or over-extended), or below the lower band (sharp decline or oversold).
bb_position.howCalculated: Compares current price to the upper and lower Bollinger Bands (2 standard deviations from the 20-day SMA). Three states: above the upper band ('above_upper'), inside, or below the lower band ('below_lower').

bands.text: ABOVE UPPER BAND — an unusually strong move. Could be a breakout with momentum, or over-extended and due for a pullback. Check RSI and volume.
BELOW LOWER BAND — an unusually sharp decline. Could be a buying opportunity if oversold, or a sign of serious trouble. Check fundamentals.
INSIDE BANDS — normal trading within the expected volatility range. No extreme pressure in either direction.

bb_position.whyMatters: When price touches or breaks through the bands, it signals something unusual. Combined with RSI and volume, this can indicate breakout opportunities (above upper with high volume + rising RSI) or warning signs (above upper with falling RSI + low volume).
bb_position.scoringImpact: Inside the bands = neutral. Above upper during a strong trend (ADX > 25) with confirming volume = positive. Below lower = typically negative unless other factors (RSI oversold, insider buying) suggest a bounce.
commonMistakes: Shorting just because price is above the upper band — in strong trends, price can ride the upper band for weeks.
Buying just because price is below the lower band — a falling knife can cut deeper; wait for a reversal signal.
bb_position.example: NVDA broke above the upper band in May 2023 with RSI at 65 and volume 2.5x — continued up 40% over two months. The same stock pierced the upper band in July 2022 with RSI at 82 and volume 0.8x — pulled back 15% in a week.

macd_status.label: MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence)
macd_status.oneLiner: Spots momentum shifts by comparing two moving averages — like feeling the wind change before the weather turns.
macd_status.what: MACD compares the 12-day and 26-day exponential moving averages to spot changes in momentum. The MACD line crossing above the signal line is a classic bullish signal; crossing below is bearish. It helps you catch trend changes early.
macd_status.howCalculated: MACD line = EMA12 minus EMA26. Signal line = 9-day EMA of MACD line. Status is bullish (MACD > signal), bearish (MACD < signal), or neutral (very close).

bands.text: BULLISH — the shorter-term average crossed above the longer-term one. Momentum is shifting upward. A classic buy signal.
BEARISH — the shorter-term average crossed below the longer-term one. Downward momentum is building. A warning sign.
NEUTRAL — the two averages are close together. No clear momentum signal. The stock is 'coasting' without a directional push.

macd_status.whyMatters: MACD helps you catch trend changes EARLY. It's like feeling the wind shift before the weather changes. Traders use it to time entries (bullish cross) and exits (bearish cross) rather than predicting tops and bottoms.
macd_status.scoringImpact: Bullish MACD adds to the technical score. Bearish MACD subtracts. Neutral has no impact.
commonMistakes: Trading every MACD cross in a choppy market (ADX < 20) — whipsaws will bleed the account.
Ignoring the histogram — the distance between MACD and signal line shows momentum acceleration/deceleration before the cross happens.
macd_status.example: AMD bullish MACD cross in November 2022 at $65 preceded a 60% rally over four months. Bearish cross in July 2023 at $110 preceded a 25% correction. The histogram started shrinking two weeks before the bearish cross — early warning.

avg_volume_20d.label: Avg Volume (20d)
avg_volume_20d.oneLiner: How many shares trade daily on average — the 'width of the door' for getting in and out.
avg_volume_20d.what: Average 20-day volume is the mean number of shares traded each day over the last month. Higher volume means more liquidity — you can buy or sell large positions without moving the price. Low volume means wide spreads and slippage.
avg_volume_20d.howCalculated: Sum of daily volume over 20 trading days ÷ 20.

bands.text: ${value} shares/day — very liquid. Huge volume means you can trade large positions without affecting the price.
${value} shares/day — decent liquidity. Normal for mid-to-large cap stocks.
${value} shares/day — moderate. Tradeable but larger orders may affect the price.
${value} shares/day — low volume. Be careful with position size as the spread may be wide.

avg_volume_20d.whyMatters: Volume is like the 'width' of the market. High volume = easy to get in and out. Low volume = price can move against you when you try to trade. Always check volume before buying an unfamiliar stock.
avg_volume_20d.scoringImpact: Not a scoring factor itself, but a liquidity gate: our screener templates filter out stocks under ~500K shares/day. High average volume is assumed by every other score — without it, entries/exits get unreliable.
commonMistakes: Confusing average volume with current volume — today's volume might be 10× average on news, but that doesn't make the stock 10× more liquid permanently.
Ignoring that volume tends to scale with market cap — a $10B stock trading 1M shares/day is normal; a $100M stock trading 1M shares/day is extremely active.
Not checking if volume is real — some low-float stocks show high volume from a few large trades, not broad participation.
avg_volume_20d.example: Apple trades ~50M shares/day — you can buy $1M worth instantly. A micro-cap might trade 50K shares/day — a $10K order could move the price 5%. The screener's '×2.3' volume badge uses current volume vs this 20-day average.

sma_50_200.label: SMA 50/200 (Golden Cross / Death Cross)
sma_50_200.oneLiner: The 50-day vs 200-day moving average crossover — one of the most watched long-term trend signals in the market.
sma_50_200.what: Compares the 50-day moving average to the 200-day moving average. When the 50-day crosses ABOVE the 200-day, it's called a 'Golden Cross' — historically bullish. When it crosses BELOW, it's a 'Death Cross' — historically bearish. These don't happen often, so when they do, traders pay attention.
sma_50_200.howCalculated: Simple comparison of SMA50 and SMA200. Golden Cross = SMA50 crosses above SMA200. Death Cross = SMA50 crosses below SMA200. No cross = neither has occurred recently.

bands.text: GOLDEN CROSS — the 50-day average crossed ABOVE the 200-day! This is one of the most reliable bullish signals. Short-term trend is now stronger than long-term.
DEATH CROSS — the 50-day average crossed BELOW the 200-day. A serious bearish signal. Short-term trend has broken down; the stock may be entering a downtrend.
NO CROSS — the 50 and 200-day averages are maintaining their current order. No extreme trend change signal right now.

sma_50_200.whyMatters: Golden Crosses historically precede major bull runs. Death Crosses often (but not always) precede bear markets. They don't happen often, so when they do, pay attention — but confirm with other indicators.
sma_50_200.scoringImpact: Golden Cross = strong positive score boost. Death Cross = strong negative. No cross = neutral. This is a high-impact signal that can override other factors.
commonMistakes: Trading the cross in isolation — many Death Crosses in 2022 were followed by rallies (false signals in a bear market rally).
Expecting immediate moves — crosses are long-term signals; the payoff can take months.
sma_50_200.example: S&P 500 Golden Cross in April 2019 preceded a 35% rally over 18 months. Death Cross in March 2020 was a false signal — the market bottomed days later and rallied 100%+. Context (Fed policy, earnings) matters more than the cross alone.

consecutive_gains.label: Consecutive Gains
consecutive_gains.oneLiner: How many days in a row the stock closed higher — a streak shows momentum, but long streaks often end with a pullback.
consecutive_gains.what: The number of consecutive trading days the stock has closed higher than the previous day. A streak of up days shows persistent buying pressure. Think of it like a winning streak in sports — it shows the team is playing well, but the longer it goes, the more 'due' a loss feels.
consecutive_gains.howCalculated: Counts sequential days where close > previous close. Resets to 0 on a down day (or negative).

bands.text: ${value} days — EXCEPTIONAL streak! Over a week straight up. Intense buying pressure, but statistically due for a breather or pullback.
${value} days — STRONG streak. A full trading week of gains. Clear bullish momentum.
${value} days — MODERATE streak. Three up days in a row is a positive short-term momentum signal.
${value} day — JUST STARTED. One up day doesn't make a trend, but it's a start.
${value} days — DECLINING. The stock has been going down recently. Check other indicators for context.

consecutive_gains.whyMatters: Streaks show momentum. A stock that keeps going up day after day has strong buying pressure. But beware: long streaks (7+) often end with a pullback. The longer the streak, the closer the potential reversal — like a rubber band stretched too far.
consecutive_gains.scoringImpact: Moderate streaks (3–5 days) add to the momentum score. Very long streaks (7+) can be a double-edged sword — strong momentum but higher pullback risk.
commonMistakes: Chasing a 7+ day streak thinking 'it keeps going up' — statistically, mean reversion risk rises sharply after 5–7 days.
Ignoring the magnitude — 5 days of +0.2% gains is not the same as 5 days of +2% gains.
consecutive_gains.example: NVDA had 8 consecutive up days in May 2023 (AI rally) — gained 22% during the streak, then pulled back 8% over the next week. A 3-day streak in a boring utility stock might mean nothing.

change_1w.label: 1-Week Change
change_1w.oneLiner: The stock's percentage move over the last 5 trading days — a snapshot of recent momentum.
change_1w.what: Shows how much the stock has moved (up or down) over the past 5 trading days (one week). It's a quick pulse check on recent momentum. A +5% week means the stock gained 5% in five sessions; -3% means it lost 3%.
change_1w.howCalculated: (Current price - Price 5 trading days ago) / Price 5 trading days ago × 100. Expressed as a percentage.

bands.text: ${value}% — EXCEPTIONAL weekly gain. The stock surged. Check for news, earnings, or a breakout. May be extended short-term.
${value}% — STRONG weekly gain. Solid momentum. Confirm with volume and trend alignment.
${value}% — MODERATE gain. Normal positive week. Nothing unusual.
${value}% — FLAT week. Minimal net change. The stock drifted sideways.
${value}% — MODERATE decline. Normal pullback in an uptrend or continued weakness.
${value}% — STRONG weekly loss. Significant selling pressure. Check for news or trend break.
${value}% — SEVERE weekly decline. Major selling. Could be a crash, bad earnings, or sector rotation. High risk.

change_1w.whyMatters: A strong weekly move can signal the start of a new trend, the acceleration of an existing one, or an overbought/oversold extreme. It's the 'what happened this week' summary that contextualizes daily moves.
change_1w.scoringImpact: Positive weekly changes (+2% to +5%) add to the momentum score. Extreme weekly moves (>10% either direction) are scrutinized for sustainability — often mean-reversion candidates.
commonMistakes: Reacting to a single week's move without checking the broader trend (monthly, quarterly).
Confusing a 1-week change with a 1-month or 1-year change — timeframe matters enormously.
change_1w.example: META +12% in one week after Q1 2023 earnings — confirmed a trend reversal from the 2022 bear market. The same week, a small biotech +15% on FDA approval news — but volume was 0.5x average, and it gave back all gains in two weeks.

beta.label: Beta (Market Correlation)
beta.oneLiner: How much the stock amplifies or dampens market moves — your risk thermostat for portfolio construction.
beta.what: Beta measures how much the stock moves compared to the overall market (S&P 500). A beta of 1 means the stock moves in line with the market. A beta of 1.5 means it moves 50% more than the market — if the S&P rises 1%, this stock tends to rise 1.5%. A beta of 0.5 means it moves half as much. Negative beta means it moves opposite the market (rare).
beta.howCalculated: Regression of the stock's daily returns against S&P 500 daily returns over a lookback period (typically 1–2 years). The slope coefficient is beta.

bands.text: ${value} — HIGH beta. The stock amplifies market moves. If the market goes up 1%, this stock often goes up 1.5%+. But it also falls harder. Aggressive risk profile.
${value} — above-market beta. Moves more than the S&P but not extremely. Growth stocks often sit here.
${value} — MARKET-LIKE beta. Moves roughly in line with the overall market. Typical for most large-cap stocks.
${value} — LOW beta. The stock is more stable than the market. Good for defensive/conservative positioning. Utilities, consumer staples often here.
${value} — VERY LOW or NEGATIVE beta. The stock barely reacts to the market or moves opposite to it. Rare — found in gold miners, deep value, or heavily distressed names.

beta.whyMatters: Beta helps you understand a stock's risk profile and how it will behave in your portfolio. High beta = high risk, high reward. Low beta = stable but less upside. If you're building a portfolio, mixing high and low beta stocks balances risk — like mixing spicy and mild dishes.
beta.scoringImpact: High beta (>1.5) is a slight negative (more risk). Low beta (<0.8) is a slight positive (more stable). Market-like beta (0.8–1.3) is neutral. Combined with other risk metrics.
commonMistakes: Assuming low beta means 'safe' — a low-beta stock can still crash on company-specific news (earnings miss, fraud, product failure).
Using beta as a predictor — it describes past correlation, not future causation. Correlations change during crises (everything correlates to 1 in a crash).
beta.example: NVDA beta ~1.8 — in 2022 when S&P fell 19%, NVDA fell ~50%. In 2023 when S&P rose 24%, NVDA rose ~240%. JNJ beta ~0.6 — in 2022 fell only ~5%; in 2023 rose ~10%. Beta predicts the 'gearing' to market moves.

market_regime.label: Market Regime
market_regime.oneLiner: The current 'weather' of the overall market — bull, bear, choppy, or crisis — so you can match your strategy to the environment.
market_regime.what: Market regime classifies the broad market environment into categories like bull market (rising with low volatility), bear market (falling), choppy/range-bound (no clear direction), or crisis (high volatility, panic). Just as you dress differently for summer vs. winter, you trade differently in a bull vs. bear regime.
market_regime.howCalculated: Combines S&P 500 trend (price vs. moving averages), breadth (advance/decline), volatility (VIX), and momentum indicators into a regime classification.

bands.text: STRONG BULL MARKET — uptrend with low volatility and broad participation. Favorable for trend-following and growth strategies.
WEAK BULL MARKET — uptrend but narrowing breadth or rising volatility. Be selective; avoid chasing.
CHOPPY / RANGE-BOUND — no clear direction. Whipsaws common. Mean-reversion and range-trading work better than trend-following.
BEAR MARKET — sustained downtrend. Defensive positioning, cash raising, or short strategies favored. Long-only entries need strong catalysts.
CRISIS / PANIC — extreme volatility, forced selling, correlation convergence to 1. Capital preservation is priority. Most strategies fail here.
${value} — regime unclear or transitioning. Reduce size and wait for clarity.

market_regime.whyMatters: Your strategy must match the regime. Buying breakouts in a bear market is like surfing in a hurricane — you'll get crushed. Shorting in a strong bull is like standing in front of a freight train. Regime awareness is the single biggest edge for swing traders.
market_regime.scoringImpact: Regime acts as a portfolio-level filter. Bull regimes boost conviction thresholds for longs. Bear regimes raise dealbreaker sensitivity. Crisis regime can disable new entries entirely.
commonMistakes: Using the same strategy in all regimes — a trend-following system that works in a bull market loses money in a choppy market.
Ignoring regime transitions — the market often gives warning signs (breadth divergence, VIX spikes) weeks before a regime shift.
market_regime.example: 2021: Strong bull regime — trend-following on growth stocks worked beautifully. 2022: Bear regime — the same strategy lost 30%+. 2023 H1: Bull regime returned — trend-following worked again. Traders who adapted to regime survived; those who didn't blew up.

sector_rotation.label: Sector Rotation
sector_rotation.oneLiner: Which sectors are leading or lagging — tells you where the big money is flowing right now.
sector_rotation.what: Sector rotation tracks which industry groups are outperforming or underperforming the market. Money flows from sector to sector like seasons — tech leads in early expansion, energy in late cycle, utilities in downturns. Knowing the current rotation helps you fish where the fish are.
sector_rotation.howCalculated: Compares each sector ETF's performance (e.g., XLK, XLE, XLF) against the S&P 500 over multiple timeframes (1-week, 1-month, 3-month). Ranks sectors by relative strength.

bands.text: TECHNOLOGY LEADING — growth sectors outperforming. Risk-on environment. Favorable for momentum and growth strategies.
DEFENSIVE LEADING (utilities, staples, healthcare) — risk-off environment. Money seeking safety. Favorable for dividend/value strategies.
CYCLICALS LEADING (financials, industrials, materials) — economic expansion expectations. Early-to-mid cycle signal.
ENERGY LEADING — often late-cycle or inflation-driven. Commodity strength benefiting producers.
${value} — mixed or unclear rotation. No dominant sector theme. Stock-picking matters more than sector bets.

sector_rotation.whyMatters: A rising tide lifts most boats, but the *fastest* boats are in the leading sectors. Buying a strong stock in a lagging sector is swimming upstream. Sector tailwinds can add 5–15% annualized alpha over random selection.
sector_rotation.scoringImpact: Stocks in leading sectors get a sentiment boost. Stocks in lagging sectors face a higher bar for entry. Sector rotation is a moderate-weight factor in the overall score.
commonMistakes: Chasing yesterday's leading sector — rotation moves fast; by the time retail notices, smart money is rotating out.
Ignoring sector context — a 'great chart' in a hated sector often fails, while a 'mediocre chart' in a loved sector rips.
sector_rotation.example: 2022: Energy (XLE) +60% while Tech (XLK) -30% — rotating into energy early was the trade. 2023: Tech +50%, Energy -5% — rotation flipped. Traders who stayed in energy 'because it worked last year' missed the tech rally.

vix.label: VIX (Volatility Index)
vix.oneLiner: The market's 'fear gauge' — measures expected 30-day volatility from S&P 500 options. Low = complacency; high = panic.
vix.what: The VIX (CBOE Volatility Index) measures the market's expectation of 30-day volatility, derived from S&P 500 option prices. It's called the 'fear gauge' because it spikes when investors are scared and buy protection (puts). Below 15 = calm/complacent; 15–25 = normal; 25–35 = nervous; above 35 = panic/fear.
vix.howCalculated: Model-free implied volatility from a strip of S&P 500 options across strikes and expirations, annualized. Quoted in percentage points (e.g., VIX 18 = 18% expected annualized volatility).

bands.text: ${value} — EXTREMELY CALM. Complacency is high. Markets often top out near VIX lows. 'Buy the dip' mentality dominates.
${value} — CALM. Low fear, steady uptrend typical. Good for trend-following but watch for complacency.
${value} — NORMAL. Balanced fear/greed. Typical trading environment.
${value} — ELEVATED. Nervousness rising. Pullbacks more frequent. Tighten stops, reduce size.
${value} — HIGH FEAR. Significant uncertainty. Sharp moves both ways. Difficult for directional strategies.
${value} — PANIC / CRISIS. Extreme fear. Forced liquidation, margin calls. Capital preservation mode. Most strategies break.

vix.whyMatters: VIX is the market's heart rate monitor. Low VIX = market is relaxed (often near tops). High VIX = market is stressed (often near bottoms). But VIX can stay elevated for weeks in a crisis — don't try to catch a falling knife just because VIX is high.
vix.scoringImpact: Low VIX (<15) slightly reduces dealbreaker thresholds (market is forgiving). High VIX (>30) tightens dealbreakers and reduces position sizes. VIX > 40 can trigger portfolio-level risk-off.
commonMistakes: Thinking VIX predicts direction — it predicts *magnitude* of moves, not direction. High VIX means big moves coming; could be up or down.
Shorting VIX (selling volatility) as a 'free money' strategy — works until it doesn't. VIX spikes can wipe out months of gains in days.
vix.example: VIX 12 in January 2018 — market topped weeks later. VIX 82 in March 2020 — market bottomed that week. VIX 35 in October 2022 — bear market low. VIX is best used as a contrarian *context* tool, not a timing signal.

advance_decline_ratio.label: Advance/Decline Ratio
advance_decline_ratio.oneLiner: The ratio of advancing to declining stocks — shows whether a rally is broad (healthy) or narrow (fragile).
advance_decline_ratio.what: Counts how many stocks went up vs. down on a given day. A ratio of 2.0 means two stocks advanced for every one that declined. A ratio above 1 = more gainers than losers; below 1 = more losers. Broad participation (ratio > 2) confirms a healthy trend; narrow participation (ratio < 1 while index rises) is a divergence warning.
advance_decline_ratio.howCalculated: Number of advancing issues divided by number of declining issues on the NYSE/NASDAQ. Can be daily, weekly, or cumulative (advance/decline line).

bands.text: ${value} — VERY BROAD participation. Over 3 advancers per decliner. Extremely healthy breadth. Strong bullish confirmation.
${value} — BROAD participation. Most stocks rising with the index. Trend is confirmed by the 'troops'.
${value} — POSITIVE but narrowing. More advancers than decliners, but not overwhelmingly. Monitor for divergence.
${value} — NEGATIVE breadth. More decliners than advancers. If the index is rising, this is a BEARISH DIVERGENCE — few stocks carrying the load.
${value} — VERY NEGATIVE breadth. Severe selling pressure across the board. Confirms downtrend or panic.

advance_decline_ratio.whyMatters: A rally led by 5 mega-caps while 80% of stocks fall is a 'fake out' — the generals are advancing but the army is retreating. Broad participation means the move has legs; narrow participation means it's vulnerable.
advance_decline_ratio.scoringImpact: Broad A/D (>2) adds to market regime bullishness. Negative A/D (<1) with rising index is a dealbreaker flag for new longs. Used in market_regime classification.
commonMistakes: Watching only the S&P 500 level — the index can rise on 5 stocks while 495 fall. That's not a bull market.
Using daily A/D alone — too noisy. Look at the cumulative A/D line or 5–10 day averages for signal.
advance_decline_ratio.example: January 2022: S&P 500 made a new high but A/D ratio was 0.6 — only 37% of stocks participating. Classic divergence. The index peaked days later and fell 25%. June 2023: S&P 500 broke out with A/D ratio 3.2 — broad participation confirmed the new bull leg.

dollar_index.label: Dollar Index (DXY)
dollar_index.oneLiner: The US dollar's value vs. a basket of major currencies — a stronger dollar hurts multinational earnings and commodities.
dollar_index.what: The Dollar Index (DXY) measures the US dollar against a basket of six major currencies (euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona, Swiss franc). A rising DXY means the dollar is strengthening. This matters because: (1) ~40% of S&P 500 revenue is overseas — a strong dollar reduces those earnings when converted back to USD; (2) commodities are priced in dollars — strong dollar = lower commodity prices; (3) emerging markets borrow in dollars — strong dollar = debt stress.
dollar_index.howCalculated: Geometric weighted average of the six currency pairs. Index started at 100 in 1973. Current level reflects dollar strength/weakness since then.

bands.text: ${value} — VERY STRONG dollar. Headwind for multinational earnings and commodities. Favorable for domestic-focused small caps.
${value} — STRONG dollar. Modest headwind for international earnings. Monitor commodity exposure.
${value} — NEUTRAL zone. Dollar neither a significant help nor hindrance. Normal range for recent years.
${value} — WEAK dollar. Tailwind for multinational earnings and commodities. Emerging markets benefit.
${value} — VERY WEAK dollar. Strong tailwind for international revenue and commodities. Inflation risk rises.

dollar_index.whyMatters: The dollar is the 'denominator' for global assets. When DXY rises, it's like the tide going out — exposes who's swimming naked (high foreign revenue, high dollar debt). Sector rotation often follows dollar turns: weak dollar helps energy, materials, tech (international); strong dollar helps domestic retailers, utilities, regional banks.
dollar_index.scoringImpact: Strong DXY (>105) is a slight negative for large-cap tech/multinationals. Weak DXY (<95) is a slight positive for the same. Used in sector_rotation and market_regime context.
commonMistakes: Assuming strong dollar is always 'bad for stocks' — domestic companies with no foreign revenue benefit from cheaper imports.
Ignoring the *rate of change* — a dollar that rises 5% in a month hurts earnings more than one that rises 5% over a year (companies hedge).
dollar_index.example: DXY 114 in September 2022 — S&P 500 earnings estimates cut 5–10% for high-international-revenue names. DXY 90 in July 2023 — same companies raised guidance. The dollar moved 20% in 10 months; earnings followed.

sp500_futures.label: S&P 500 Futures
sp500_futures.oneLiner: Pre-market and after-hours price action for the S&P 500 — the overnight 'preview' of where the market will open.
sp500_futures.what: S&P 500 futures (E-mini, ticker /ES) trade nearly 24/7 and indicate where the cash market will open. If futures are up 0.5% at 8 AM ET, the market will likely open higher. They reflect global news, earnings, and positioning while the US market is closed.
sp500_futures.howCalculated: Fair value of the S&P 500 index based on the front-month futures contract, adjusted for dividends and interest rates. Quoted in index points (e.g., 4500).

bands.text: ${value}% — futures UP significantly. Positive overnight catalyst (earnings, data, geopolitical). Expect gap-up open.
${value}% — futures modestly UP. Slight positive bias. Normal overnight drift.
${value}% — futures FLAT. No strong overnight signal. Open likely near prior close.
${value}% — futures modestly DOWN. Slight negative bias. Normal overnight drift.
${value}% — futures DOWN significantly. Negative overnight catalyst. Expect gap-down open. Check news.

sp500_futures.whyMatters: Futures set the opening tone. A gap up on high volume often leads to follow-through; a gap down can trigger stop-loss cascades. Swing traders use futures to size positions before the open — if futures are -1%, you might reduce new long size.
sp500_futures.scoringImpact: Used for pre-market position sizing and entry timing. Not a direct scoring factor but influences execution. Large gap (>1%) triggers dealbreaker review for pending entries.
commonMistakes: Trading the futures move directly — futures are for hedging/institutional access; retail should wait for the cash open for liquidity.
Assuming futures predict the *day's close* — they only predict the *open*. The market often reverses the futures move by 10 AM.
sp500_futures.example: NVDA earnings May 2023: futures +1.5% pre-market on blowout guide. Market opened +1.2%, closed +3%. Same quarter 2022: futures -2% on miss; opened -2.5%, closed -5%. Futures direction matched the day's direction 70%+ of earnings days.

nasdaq_futures.label: Nasdaq 100 Futures
nasdaq_futures.oneLiner: Pre-market/after-hours for the Nasdaq 100 — more tech-heavy and volatile than S&P futures.
nasdaq_futures.what: Nasdaq 100 futures (/NQ) track the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 index. They trade 24/7 like S&P futures but are more volatile because tech stocks have higher beta. A 1% move in /ES often means a 1.5% move in /NQ. Tech traders watch /NQ more closely.
nasdaq_futures.howCalculated: Fair value of the Nasdaq 100 index based on the front-month futures contract. Quoted in index points (e.g., 15000).

bands.text: ${value}% — /NQ UP significantly. Tech sentiment very positive. Expect gap-up in growth names.
${value}% — /NQ modestly UP. Slight positive tech bias.
${value}% — /NQ FLAT. No strong tech-specific overnight signal.
${value}% — /NQ modestly DOWN. Slight negative tech bias.
${value}% — /NQ DOWN significantly. Tech sentiment negative. Growth stocks likely to gap down.

nasdaq_futures.whyMatters: If you trade tech/growth stocks, /NQ is your pre-market compass. It often leads /ES (S&P futures) on tech-specific news (AI announcements, chip earnings, Fed tech-sensitive policy). Divergence between /NQ and /ES (e.g., /NQ up 1%, /ES flat) signals sector rotation into tech.
nasdaq_futures.scoringImpact: Used for pre-market tech-position sizing. Not a direct scoring factor. Large /NQ gap (>1.5%) triggers dealbreaker review for pending tech longs.
commonMistakes: Using /NQ for non-tech stocks — a bank stock doesn't care about /NQ nearly as much as /ES.
Overreacting to /NQ moves — higher beta means more noise. A 1% /NQ move can reverse in the first 15 minutes.
nasdaq_futures.example: ChatGPT launch Nov 2022: /NQ futures +3% pre-market on Microsoft/OpenAI news. /ES only +0.8%. Tech leadership confirmed. Feb 2025: DeepSeek news — /NQ -2.5% pre-market, /ES -0.8%. Tech-specific panic.

market_cap.label: Market Cap
market_cap.oneLiner: The total value of all the company's shares — the price tag for buying the whole company.
market_cap.what: Market cap is the stock price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding. It tells you how big the company is, like a price tag on the entire business. A $10 billion company is considered mid-cap, while $200 billion+ puts it in mega-cap territory alongside Apple and Microsoft.
market_cap.howCalculated: Current stock price × total shares outstanding.

bands.text: ${value}B — mega-cap giant. One of the largest companies in the world, extremely stable but slower growth.
${value}B — large-cap. Established industry leader with proven business model and steady growth.
${value}B — mid-cap. Growing company with room to expand, moderate risk.
${value}B — small-cap. Younger company with high growth potential but higher risk of failure.
${value}B — micro-cap. Very small company, speculative investment with significant risk.

market_cap.whyMatters: Company size affects risk and return profile. Large caps are stable but grow slower; small caps can multiply but can also disappear. Your strategy should match the size tier.
market_cap.scoringImpact: Market cap doesn't directly add or subtract from the score, but very small caps (<$50M) with poor profitability are flagged as a dealbreaker — too risky.
commonMistakes: Comparing market caps across different industries without context — a $10B bank is tiny compared to a $10B tech company.
Assuming a low market cap automatically means 'undervalued' — many micro-caps are small for good reason.
Ignoring that market cap changes daily with the stock price — it's not a fixed attribute of the company.
market_cap.example: If a stock trades at $50 with 2 billion shares outstanding, its market cap is $100 billion — a large-cap company. If the same company had 100 million shares at $50, it would be a $5 billion mid-cap.

pe_ratio.label: P/E Ratio (Price to Earnings)
pe_ratio.oneLiner: How many dollars you pay for each dollar of the company's annual profit — like a price tag on earnings.
pe_ratio.what: The P/E ratio divides the stock price by earnings per share. If a stock trades at $100 with $5 EPS, the P/E is 20 — you're paying $20 for every $1 of yearly profit. Think of it like a price-to-rent ratio for a house: lower means cheaper, but you need to know why.
pe_ratio.howCalculated: Stock price ÷ earnings per share (EPS). Can use trailing (last 12 months) or forward (estimated next 12 months) earnings.

bands.text: ${value} — very expensive. Investors expect explosive growth. If growth disappoints, the stock can drop sharply.
${value} — above average. The market is optimistic about future growth. Reasonable for quality growing companies.
${value} — moderate to low. The stock is reasonably priced relative to current earnings. Could be a value opportunity or the market sees problems ahead.
${value} — negative. The company is losing money. Common for early-stage growth companies, but means P/E is not useful for valuation here.

pe_ratio.whyMatters: P/E is the most common valuation shortcut. A high P/E means you're paying a premium — you need strong growth to justify it. A low P/E can mean a bargain or a value trap where the business is declining.
pe_ratio.scoringImpact: Very high P/E (>50) without strong growth = negative. Reasonable P/E (10-25) = positive. Negative P/E = neutral (common for growth companies).
commonMistakes: Comparing P/E ratios across different sectors — banks trade at 10× earnings while software trades at 30×, both can be fairly valued.
Using trailing P/E for a company whose earnings just collapsed — forward P/E is more relevant.
Assuming a low P/E is automatically cheap — a stock at 5× earnings might be heading to zero.
pe_ratio.example: Company A earns $2/share and trades at $40 → P/E of 20. Company B earns $2/share and trades at $100 → P/E of 50. Company B needs to grow earnings 2.5× faster just to catch up to Company A's valuation.

eps.label: EPS (Earnings Per Share)
eps.oneLiner: How much profit each share of stock 'owns' — the company's profit divided by its share count.
eps.what: EPS takes the company's net income and divides it by the number of shares. If a company earns $1 billion with 100 million shares, EPS is $10. It's the per-share slice of profit. Consistent EPS growth over years is a hallmark of quality companies.
eps.howCalculated: Net income ÷ weighted average shares outstanding. Diluted EPS includes potential shares from options and convertibles.

bands.text: ${value} — high EPS. Substantial profit per share, typical of mature profitable companies.
${value} — positive EPS. The company is profitable on a per-share basis.
${value} — small but positive EPS. Barely profitable per share.
${value} — negative EPS. The company lost money per share. Common for growth companies investing heavily.

eps.whyMatters: EPS is the foundation of stock value. Over the long run, stock prices follow earnings. If EPS keeps growing, the stock price usually follows. It's also the denominator for P/E ratio.
eps.scoringImpact: Positive and growing EPS = positive score contribution. Negative EPS = neutral (common in early-stage companies).
commonMistakes: Ignoring share count changes — if a company issues lots of new shares, EPS can fall even if total profit rises.
Focusing only on current EPS without looking at the growth trajectory — a company with $1 EPS growing 20% yearly is better than $5 EPS shrinking 10%.
Confusing basic vs diluted EPS — always use diluted for a conservative view.
eps.example: Apple earned $6.11 per share in 2023. At a $180 stock price, that's a P/E of about 29. If Apple grows EPS to $8 next year and the P/E stays at 29, the stock would be worth ~$232.

profit_margin.label: Profit Margin
profit_margin.oneLiner: The percentage of every revenue dollar the company keeps as profit — its pricing power and efficiency score.
profit_margin.what: Profit margin is net income divided by revenue, expressed as a percentage. If a company has $100 million in sales and $20 million in profit, its margin is 20%. It's like asking: for every dollar a customer pays, how many cents does the owner keep?

bands.text: ${value} — excellent! The company is very efficient at turning revenue into profit.
${value} — good. Healthy profitability with room to grow.
${value} — positive but thin. The company is profitable but doesn't keep much from each sale.
${value} — negative. The company spends more than it earns. Common for young/high-growth companies.

profit_margin.whyMatters: Profit margin shows how much pricing power and efficiency a company has. High margins = strong competitive advantage (like software companies with near-zero marginal cost). Low margins = tough business (like grocery stores competing on price).
profit_margin.scoringImpact: Positive margins contribute to the score. Negative margins with small market cap triggers a dealbreaker. High margins = strong positive.
commonMistakes: Comparing margins across industries — a 5% margin is great for a grocery store but terrible for a software company.
Ignoring that margins can be temporarily depressed by one-time charges or investment cycles.
Assuming high margins will persist forever — competition eventually erodes excess profits.
profit_margin.example: Microsoft has ~35% net profit margin — for every $100 of Windows/Office/Cloud sales, $35 becomes profit. Walmart has ~2.5% margin — for every $100 of groceries sold, only $2.50 is profit. Both are successful but in completely different ways.

operating_margin.label: Operating Margin
operating_margin.oneLiner: Profit from core operations before interest and taxes — how efficient the actual business is.
operating_margin.what: Operating margin is operating income divided by revenue. It excludes interest on debt and taxes, so it shows how profitable the core business is regardless of how it's financed or where it's located. Think of it as the 'pure business' profitability.

bands.text: ${value} — excellent. The company's core business is highly efficient at turning revenue into operating profit.
${value} — good. Healthy operating efficiency with room to invest in growth.
${value} — adequate. The core business is profitable but not highly efficient.
${value} — thin. The company makes a small operating profit on each sale. Vulnerable to cost increases.
${value} — negative. The core business operations are losing money. Different from net loss which could include one-time items.

operating_margin.whyMatters: Operating margin focuses on the CORE business, excluding interest and taxes. It tells you if the company's products/services are fundamentally profitable, regardless of financing decisions or tax strategies. A company with great operating margin but high debt can still be a good business.
operating_margin.scoringImpact: Strong operating margins (>15%) bolster the fundamental score. Negative operating margins over multiple periods indicate the business model may not be viable.
commonMistakes: Confusing operating margin with profit margin — operating margin is higher because it excludes interest and taxes.
Ignoring that capital-intensive businesses (manufacturing, telecom) naturally have lower operating margins than asset-light businesses (software, consulting).
Not checking trends — a declining operating margin often signals rising competition or cost pressures before it hits net profit.
operating_margin.example: Google has ~30% operating margin — its search and ads business is incredibly efficient. Ford has ~5% operating margin — building cars is capital-intensive with high fixed costs. Both can be good investments at the right price.

debt_to_equity.label: D/E Ratio (Debt to Equity)
debt_to_equity.oneLiner: How much the company owes vs. what it owns — like comparing your mortgage to your home equity.
debt_to_equity.what: Debt-to-equity compares total liabilities to shareholders' equity. A D/E of 1 means the company has equal debt and equity. A D/E of 2 means it has twice as much debt as its own money. It's like a household: if you have a $200K mortgage on a $300K home, your D/E is 2 ($200K debt / $100K equity).

bands.text: ${value} — HIGH debt. The company owes a lot relative to its own money. Riskier because debt payments eat into profits.
${value} — moderate debt. Normal for most companies. Some debt is healthy — it funds growth.
${value} — low debt. Conservative financial management. Less risk, but might be growing slower.
Negative — the company has more cash than debt. Very safe financially, but unusual for growing companies.

debt_to_equity.whyMatters: Too much debt can sink a company if business slows down (like high mortgage payments if you lose your job). Too little debt might mean the company isn't investing in growth. Capital-intensive industries (utilities, real estate) naturally carry more debt.
debt_to_equity.scoringImpact: High debt (>2) is negative. Moderate debt (0.5-1.5) is neutral. Very low or negative debt = slightly positive (financially conservative).
commonMistakes: Comparing D/E across industries — banks and utilities naturally have high D/E; software companies have near zero. Both can be normal.
Ignoring that some debt is good — it amplifies returns on equity (financial leverage) and interest is tax-deductible.
Not checking debt maturity — $10B due next year is very different from $10B due in 10 years.
debt_to_equity.example: Apple has D/E ~1.5 — moderate for a mega-cap. Tesla had negative D/E (more cash than debt) after 2020. A typical utility might have D/E of 2-3 which is normal for their stable, regulated cash flows.

fcf_yield.label: FCF Yield (Free Cash Flow Yield)
fcf_yield.oneLiner: The cash the company generates after expenses as a percentage of its stock price — like a 'cash on cash' return.
fcf_yield.what: Free cash flow is the cash left after paying for everything needed to run and maintain the business (capital expenditures). FCF yield compares that cash to the company's market cap. If a company generates $5B FCF and has a $100B market cap, the yield is 5% — you're getting 5% of your investment back in cash each year.
fcf_yield.howCalculated: Free cash flow ÷ market capitalization. FCF = operating cash flow − capital expenditures.

bands.text: ${value} — HIGH. The company generates lots of cash relative to its price. A sign of a quality business.
${value} — good. Healthy cash generation.
${value} — positive but low. Generates some cash but not a huge amount.
${value} — negative. The company is burning cash. Very common for high-growth companies. Not a problem if revenue is growing fast.

fcf_yield.whyMatters: Cash is king. Companies that generate lots of free cash can invest in growth, pay dividends, buy back stock, or weather hard times. Negative FCF means they need to borrow or raise money. FCF yield is harder to manipulate than earnings.
fcf_yield.scoringImpact: Positive FCF yield = positive score contribution. Negative = neutral or slightly negative. Strong FCF yield with growth = very positive.
commonMistakes: Confusing FCF yield with dividend yield — FCF is cash generated; dividends are cash paid out. A company can have high FCF yield but pay no dividend.
Ignoring that growing companies often have negative FCF while investing heavily — Amazon had negative FCF for years while building warehouses.
Not checking if FCF is sustainable — one-time asset sales can temporarily boost FCF.
fcf_yield.example: A $50B market cap company generating $3B FCF has a 6% FCF yield. If the stock drops to $40B while FCF stays at $3B, the yield becomes 7.5% — the same cash flow is now cheaper to buy.

dividend_yield.label: Dividend Yield
dividend_yield.oneLiner: The annual dividend payment as a percentage of the stock price — like the interest rate on your stock.
dividend_yield.what: Dividend yield is the annual dividend per share divided by the current stock price. If a stock pays $2/year in dividends and trades at $50, the yield is 4%. It's the cash income you get just for owning the stock, like rent on a property.
dividend_yield.howCalculated: Annual dividends per share ÷ current stock price × 100.

bands.text: ${value} — HIGH yield. The company returns a lot of cash to shareholders. Can be a sign of a mature, stable business.
${value} — moderate yield. A reasonable income stream plus growth potential.
${value} — low or no dividend. The company reinvests profits into growth instead of paying shareholders. Normal for growth companies.

dividend_yield.whyMatters: Dividends are like rent on your stock. Some investors want regular income (retirees). Others prefer companies that reinvest for growth. Neither is better — it depends on your goals. High yield with sustainable payout is a quality signal.
dividend_yield.scoringImpact: High dividend yield with sustainable earnings = positive. No dividend = neutral (expected for growth stocks). Suspended dividend = negative flag.
commonMistakes: Chasing high yield without checking payout ratio — a 10% yield backed by 200% payout ratio is a dividend cut waiting to happen.
Assuming no dividend means a bad company — Amazon, Google, Berkshire Hathaway pay no dividends but created massive wealth.
Not realizing yield changes daily with stock price — a stock at $100 with $4 dividend has 4% yield; if it drops to $50, yield becomes 8% but the dividend didn't change.
dividend_yield.example: A utility stock at $40 paying $1.60/year = 4% yield. A tech stock at $200 paying $0.80/year = 0.4% yield. The utility is an income play; the tech stock is a growth play. Total return = price appreciation + dividends.

return_on_equity.label: ROE (Return on Equity)
return_on_equity.oneLiner: How efficiently the company turns shareholders' money into profit — the ultimate efficiency score.
return_on_equity.what: ROE measures net income as a percentage of shareholders' equity. If shareholders put in $100 million and the company earns $15 million, ROE is 15%. It's the return on the owners' investment. Warren Buffett calls it the single most important metric for judging management quality.

bands.text: ${value} — exceptional! The company generates outstanding returns from shareholders' money. Often signals a competitive moat.
${value} — strong ROE. The company is effectively deploying capital to generate profits.
${value} — decent. In line with the overall market average.
${value} — positive but below average. The company earns a return, but less than investors might get elsewhere.
${value} — negative. The company is destroying shareholder value. A serious red flag if persistent.

return_on_equity.whyMatters: ROE tells you if the company is a good steward of investor money. High ROE suggests the business has a 'moat' — something that lets it earn above-average profits. It's the metric that best captures 'quality' in a single number.
return_on_equity.scoringImpact: High ROE (>15%) contributes positively to the fundamental score. Negative ROE is a concern. It's used alongside other metrics to gauge overall financial health.
commonMistakes: Ignoring that high debt artificially inflates ROE — a company with little equity (high debt) can show huge ROE even with mediocre profits. Check ROIC (return on invested capital) for the full picture.
Comparing ROE across industries — banks target 10-15% ROE; software companies can hit 40%+. Both can be excellent.
Not checking consistency — a one-year spike from a tax benefit or asset sale isn't the same as 10 years of 20%+ ROE.
return_on_equity.example: Company A has $100M equity and earns $20M → 20% ROE. Company B has $10M equity (high debt) and earns $20M → 200% ROE. Company B looks better on ROE alone but is much riskier. ROIC would reveal the truth.

price_to_book.label: P/B Ratio (Price to Book)
price_to_book.oneLiner: Stock price vs. liquidation value — what you'd get if the company sold everything and paid all debts.
price_to_book.what: Price-to-book compares the stock price to book value per share (assets minus liabilities). It's like comparing a house's market price to its rebuild cost. A P/B of 1 means the stock trades at exactly its liquidation value. Below 1 means you're buying assets for less than they're worth on paper.
price_to_book.howCalculated: Stock price ÷ book value per share. Book value = (total assets − total liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding.

bands.text: ${value} — high premium. Investors are paying far more than the company's assets are worth. Common for tech and service companies where value is in intangibles.
${value} — above book value. The market believes the company is worth more than its physical assets. Normal for most profitable companies.
${value} — reasonable. Stock price roughly in line with asset value. Could be undervalued or just a capital-intensive business.
${value} — below book value. Potentially UNDERVALUED — the market prices the company below its asset value. Could be a bargain or a value trap.
${value} — negative book value. The company has more liabilities than assets. High risk.

price_to_book.whyMatters: P/B is useful for valuing banks, insurance companies, and asset-heavy businesses where tangible assets matter. A low P/B can indicate a bargain, but only if the company is still profitable. Very high P/B is normal for tech companies with few physical assets.
price_to_book.scoringImpact: Contributes to the overall fundamental picture but weighted less than P/E and profit margin. Very low P/B with good profitability = positive value signal.
commonMistakes: Using P/B for asset-light companies — Google's book value is mostly servers and offices; its real value is in search algorithms and user data, which aren't on the balance sheet.
Buying just because P/B < 1 — a bank trading at 0.8× book might have bad loans that aren't marked down yet (a value trap).
Ignoring that book value uses historical cost accounting — a factory bought 20 years ago for $10M might be worth $50M today but still carried at $10M.
price_to_book.example: JPMorgan trades at ~1.2× book — typical for a well-run bank. Tesla trades at ~15× book — investors pay for future growth, not current assets. A distressed retailer at 0.3× book might be a bargain or might be heading to zero.

current_ratio.label: Current Ratio
current_ratio.oneLiner: Can the company pay its bills this year? Short-term assets divided by short-term debts.
current_ratio.what: Current ratio compares current assets (cash, inventory, receivables) to current liabilities (bills due within a year). A ratio of 2 means the company has $2 in liquid assets for every $1 of near-term debt. It's a 'can they pay the rent?' check.

bands.text: ${value} — VERY healthy. The company has far more short-term assets than liabilities. A strong safety cushion.
${value} — healthy. The company can comfortably cover its short-term obligations. Standard for most businesses.
${value} — adequate. The company can just barely cover its short-term debts. Watch for any deterioration.
${value} — concerning. The company's short-term liabilities exceed its liquid assets. Could face cash flow problems if business slows.

current_ratio.whyMatters: Current ratio is a liquidity stress test. A company that can't cover its short-term bills may need to borrow at high rates or sell assets, which hurts shareholders. Below 1.0 is a warning sign for traditional businesses. Some models (subscription software) can run safely below 1.
current_ratio.scoringImpact: Current ratio < 1.0 with small market cap = dealbreaker flag. Healthy ratio (1.5-3) = positive. Very high (>5) can mean inefficient use of cash.
commonMistakes: Assuming higher is always better — a current ratio of 10 might mean the company is hoarding cash instead of investing or returning it to shareholders.
Not checking asset quality — $100M in inventory that can't be sold isn't the same as $100M in cash.
Ignoring industry norms — retailers operate with lower current ratios than manufacturers because inventory turns fast.
current_ratio.example: Company has $500M current assets and $200M current liabilities → current ratio of 2.5. If it pays off $100M of debt using cash, assets drop to $400M, liabilities to $100M → ratio improves to 4.0. But it now has less cash for operations.

revenue_growth_yoy.label: Revenue Growth (YoY)
revenue_growth_yoy.oneLiner: How fast the company's sales are growing year-over-year — the top-line expansion rate.
revenue_growth_yoy.what: Revenue growth compares this year's sales to the same period last year. It shows if the business is getting bigger. 20% growth means the company sold 20% more than a year ago. It's the most basic measure of business momentum.
revenue_growth_yoy.howCalculated: (Current period revenue − year-ago period revenue) ÷ year-ago period revenue.

bands.text: ${value} — RAPID growth. The company is expanding quickly. Exciting but can be risky if growth isn't profitable.
${value} — solid growth. Healthy expansion without being reckless. Ideal for most investors.
${value} — modest growth. The company is growing, but slowly. Could be a mature company or facing competition.
${value} — NEGATIVE growth. Sales are shrinking. This is a red flag unless there's a clear one-time reason.

revenue_growth_yoy.whyMatters: Growing revenue means more customers, more sales, a growing business. Shrinking revenue means the opposite. It's the most basic measure of business health. Revenue growth without profit growth = declining margins (bad). Both growing together = ideal.
revenue_growth_yoy.scoringImpact: Strong growth adds to the score. Negative growth subtracts. This is one of the most important fundamental factors.
commonMistakes: Celebrating revenue growth while ignoring margins — growing revenue at a loss is easy (sell $1 bills for 90¢).
Not checking if growth is organic or from acquisitions — bought revenue is less valuable than built revenue.
Comparing growth rates across different company sizes — a $10M company doubling to $20M is 100% growth; a $100B company adding $10B is only 10%.
revenue_growth_yoy.example: A SaaS company growing from $100M to $150M ARR = 50% YoY growth. A retailer growing from $50B to $52B = 4% growth. Both can be healthy depending on context.

earnings_growth_yoy.label: Earnings Growth (YoY)
earnings_growth_yoy.oneLiner: How fast profits are growing year-over-year — shows if the company is becoming more profitable as it grows.
earnings_growth_yoy.what: Earnings growth compares this year's profit to the same period last year. It shows if the company is getting MORE profitable, not just bigger. Revenue growth + earnings growth = the ideal combination (scale + efficiency).
earnings_growth_yoy.howCalculated: (Current period net income − year-ago period net income) ÷ |year-ago period net income|.

bands.text: ${value} — EXPLOSIVE growth. Earnings are growing much faster than revenue, meaning the company is becoming more efficient.
${value} — strong growth. The company is getting more profitable rapidly. A sign of a quality business.
${value} — positive growth. Earnings are heading in the right direction.
${value} — slight decline. Earnings are down a bit. Not a crisis, but worth monitoring.
${value} — significant decline. Profits are shrinking. A red flag unless there's a clear one-time reason.

earnings_growth_yoy.whyMatters: Revenue growth shows the company is getting bigger. Earnings growth shows it's getting MORE profitable. Both together = the ideal combination. Earnings growing faster than revenue means expanding margins (operating leverage).
earnings_growth_yoy.scoringImpact: Strong earnings growth adds to the fundamental score. Negative earnings growth is a concern, especially if revenue is still growing (shrinking margins).
commonMistakes: Ignoring the base effect — a company going from $1M to $2M profit shows 100% growth; from $100M to $110M shows 10%. The latter adds far more absolute profit.
Not checking if earnings growth is sustainable — one-time tax benefits, asset sales, or accounting changes can create fake growth.
Confusing earnings growth with EPS growth — share buybacks can boost EPS growth without any real earnings improvement.
earnings_growth_yoy.example: Company grows revenue 20% but earnings 40% — margins are expanding (operating leverage). Company grows revenue 20% but earnings only 5% — margins are compressing (investment phase or competition).

peg_ratio.label: PEG Ratio
peg_ratio.oneLiner: P/E divided by earnings growth rate — the growth-adjusted price tag. PEG of 1 = fair value.
peg_ratio.what: PEG ratio takes the P/E ratio and divides it by the earnings growth rate (as a percentage). It answers: 'Is this stock reasonably priced for how fast it's growing?' A P/E of 30 with 30% growth = PEG of 1 (fair). A P/E of 30 with 10% growth = PEG of 3 (expensive).
peg_ratio.howCalculated: P/E ratio ÷ earnings growth rate (%). Uses forward P/E and estimated growth for forward PEG.

bands.text: ${value} — negative earnings growth. The company's profits are shrinking. The low PEG is NOT a bargain — it's a warning.
${value} — UNDERVALUED relative to growth. The stock's price is low compared to how fast earnings are growing. Often a good sign.
${value} — fairly valued. The price is reasonable for the growth rate. No obvious bargain or overvaluation.
${value} — OVERVALUED relative to growth. The stock's price is high compared to its growth rate. Either growth is expected to accelerate, or the stock is too expensive.

peg_ratio.whyMatters: PEG is P/E with context. A high P/E looks scary, but if the company is growing at 50% per year, a PEG of 1 means it's actually fairly priced. It's the 'growth-adjusted value' measure that lets you compare a 10× P/E slow grower to a 30× P/E fast grower.
peg_ratio.scoringImpact: PEG < 1 with positive earnings growth = strong value signal. PEG > 2 = potential overvaluation. Negative PEG = caution flag.
commonMistakes: Using trailing P/E with forward growth estimates — mismatch creates nonsense PEG. Use forward P/E with forward growth.
Trusting PEG for cyclical companies — a homebuilder at 5× P/E with -20% earnings growth has negative PEG but might be at the cycle bottom.
Ignoring that growth estimates are often wrong — analyst estimates for next year's growth are frequently off by 50%+.
peg_ratio.example: Stock A: P/E 20, growth 20% → PEG 1.0 (fair). Stock B: P/E 10, growth 5% → PEG 2.0 (expensive for growth). Stock C: P/E 40, growth 40% → PEG 1.0 (also fair). PEG lets you compare them apples-to-apples.

price_to_sales.label: P/S Ratio (Price to Sales)
price_to_sales.oneLiner: Stock price divided by revenue per share — values the company on sales, not profits. Useful for unprofitable companies.
price_to_sales.what: P/S ratio is market cap divided by revenue. If a company has $10B market cap and $2B revenue, P/S = 5. You're paying $5 for every $1 of sales. It's useful when P/E is meaningless (negative earnings), like for early-stage growth companies.
price_to_sales.howCalculated: Market capitalization ÷ total revenue. Or: stock price ÷ revenue per share.

bands.text: ${value} — very high. Common for high-growth tech companies. Investors are paying a huge premium for future revenue. High risk if growth slows.
${value} — above average. The market is optimistic about future growth. Reasonable for growth companies.
${value} — typical range. Normal valuation for most businesses.
${value} — low. The company's sales are valued conservatively. Could be a bargain or a value trap.
${value} — negative (unusual). The company has negative revenue? This is very rare — likely a data issue.

price_to_sales.whyMatters: P/S is useful for young companies that aren't profitable yet (they have P/E but it's often negative/meaningless). It tells you how much you're paying for each dollar of sales, regardless of profitability. Low P/S with high growth = potential bargain.
price_to_sales.scoringImpact: Very high P/S (>20) with slow revenue growth = overvalued. Low P/S with high revenue growth = potential bargain. No direct score impact for unprofitable companies — assessed alongside growth rate.
commonMistakes: Comparing P/S across industries — software companies trade at 10-20× sales; retailers at 0.5-1×. Both can be fairly valued.
Ignoring margins — two companies with same P/S but one has 30% margin and the other 5%. The high-margin one deserves higher P/S.
Using P/S for mature companies — P/E is better when earnings are positive and stable. P/S ignores profitability entirely.
price_to_sales.example: Cloud software company: $20B market cap, $1B revenue → P/S 20. Mature retailer: $50B market cap, $100B revenue → P/S 0.5. The software company is priced for 50%+ growth; the retailer for 2% growth. Both P/S ratios make sense in context.

institutional_flow.label: Institutional Flow
institutional_flow.oneLiner: Net buying or selling by big money (funds, pensions, hedgies) last month — the smart money's verdict.
institutional_flow.what: Institutional flow tracks whether large institutions are net buyers or sellers of the stock over the past month. Positive means more buying than selling. These are professional investors with research teams — their actions reveal conviction.
institutional_flow.howCalculated: Net shares bought by institutions − net shares sold by institutions over the reporting period, normalized.

bands.text: ${value} — STRONG institutional buying. Major investors are accumulating shares. One of the most bullish signals available.
${value} — moderate buying. Institutions are adding to positions. Mildly bullish.
${value} — neutral. No significant institutional activity this month.
${value} — moderate selling. Institutions are reducing positions. Mildly bearish.
${value} — STRONG institutional selling. Smart money is getting out. A significant warning sign.

institutional_flow.whyMatters: Institutions do extensive research before making moves. When they're consistently buying a stock, it's because their analysts found something compelling. When they're all selling, pay attention. This is real money voting with their feet.
institutional_flow.scoringImpact: Strong buying = significant positive boost. Strong selling = significant negative. This is weighted heavily in sentiment because it represents real money in action.
commonMistakes: Confusing flow with ownership — high institutional ownership means they already own it; flow tells you if they're adding or reducing.
Not checking the timeframe — monthly flow can be noisy. Quarterly trends are more meaningful.
Assuming institutions are always right — they herd, they make mistakes, and they have different time horizons than you.
institutional_flow.example: Stock shows +8 institutional flow last month — several large funds added positions. Next month shows -6 — the same funds are taking profits. The trend matters more than any single month.

last_surprise_pct.label: Earnings Surprise
last_surprise_pct.oneLiner: How much a company's actual profit beat or missed analyst predictions, shown as a percentage.
last_surprise_pct.what: Think of it as a quarterly report card for profits. Analysts guess what a company will earn. The surprise is how far the real answer is from those guesses, in either direction. A big beat is like the student who aced a test everyone said they would barely pass; a big miss is the opposite.
last_surprise_pct.howCalculated: Compares actual earnings per share to the consensus analyst estimate for the same quarter.

bands.text: ${value} — BIG BEAT. The company crushed expectations by a wide margin. Often a strong catalyst that pushes the stock price higher the next session.
${value} — beat. The company outperformed estimates. Positive but the magnitude determines how much impact.
${value} — slight miss. Small enough that many investors shrug it off if the rest of the story still looks good.
${value} — BIG MISS. Significantly below expectations. Usually a negative catalyst that weighs on the stock price.

last_surprise_pct.whyMatters: Consistent beaters tend to earn repeat positive moves, while consistent missers disappoint repeatedly. One quarter alone is noise; a track record is signal.
last_surprise_pct.scoringImpact: Positive surprises add points. Large negative surprises deduct points. Repeated strong beaters score higher over time.
commonMistakes: Treating one big beat as proof future earnings will keep growing — surprises can be one-time.
Ignoring why a miss happened — some misses come from profitable investments that will pay off later.
last_surprise_pct.example: A company estimates $1.00 EPS but reports $1.12: a +12% surprise, landing in the BIG BEAT band. The next quarter it estimates $1.05 but reports $1.03: a -2% surprise, landing in the slight-miss band.

beat_rate.label: Beat Rate
beat_rate.oneLiner: How many recent quarterly reports the company exceeded analyst expectations.
beat_rate.what: One great quarter could be luck. A beat rate asks: out of the last several earnings reports, how many times did the company outperform? A 4-out-of-4 record means the business consistently delivers; a 1-out-of-4 record suggests execution problems.
beat_rate.howCalculated: Counts recent quarters where actual earnings per share exceeded the consensus estimate, then expresses it as a fraction or percentage.

bands.text: ${value} quarters — strong beat rate. Most recent reports exceeded expectations, signaling reliable execution.
${value} quarters — moderate beat rate. The company beats slightly more often than it misses.
${value} quarter — low beat rate. Beats are the exception, not the rule.
${value} quarters — zero beats. The company has not topped expectations in recent history.
${value} — beat rate. Review the last few quarters to see the pattern.

beat_rate.whyMatters: A high beat rate suggests the business has real momentum. A low beat rate suggests the company consistently underperforms what Wall Street expects.
beat_rate.scoringImpact: High beat rate (3+ out of 4) is a strong positive. Low beat rate (0–1 out of 4) is negative. This is one of the more reliable quality indicators.
commonMistakes: Confusing a single big beat with a dependable pattern — one quarter is not a trend.
Ignoring guidance changes — a company might beat recent estimates but lower future guidance, which matters more.
beat_rate.example: A stock with a 3-out-of-4 beat rate recently delivered positive surprises in three of its last four quarters. That track record earns a positive weight in the earnings score.

next_earnings_date.label: Next Earnings Date
next_earnings_date.oneLiner: The scheduled day the company will release its next quarterly profit report.
next_earnings_date.what: Earnings day functions like a company-wide status update: stock prices can gap up or down 10–20% in minutes depending on the numbers. This value simply marks the calendar event so you can plan around the likely volatility without being surprised.
next_earnings_date.howCalculated: Based on the company's historical reporting schedule, confirmed against analyst calendars and official company investor-relations pages.
next_earnings_date.whyMatters: If a stock jumps 15% overnight after earnings, stop-loss orders may not execute at your intended price. Knowing the date lets you reduce upcoming position size or wait until the report passes before entering.
next_earnings_date.scoringImpact: Does not directly change the score. It is informational so you can make smarter timing decisions.
commonMistakes: Buying right before earnings hoping for a positive gap — that is lottery thinking.
Forgetting that gaps happen overnight and a limit order set during the trading day may not protect you.
next_earnings_date.example: A stock trading at $120 has earnings in five days. Many swing traders trim position size ahead of the event. If the report is a clean beat, the stock might open near $132 the next morning; a miss could open near $108.

analyst_consensus.label: Analyst Consensus
analyst_consensus.oneLiner: A blended grade from professional analysts who publish buy, hold, or sell recommendations on the stock.
analyst_consensus.what: Full-time analysts study the company's books, interview management, and model future earnings before publishing a rating. The consensus averages those ratings into one opinion. It is not gospel, but it represents the collected view of people whose job is to be right.
analyst_consensus.howCalculated: Collects all active analyst ratings for a stock, normalises them onto a common scale, and averages to a single consensus statement.

bands.text: ${value} — Wall Street is strongly bullish. Most upgraded analysts expect meaningful upside from here.
${value} — analysts are generally bullish. A majority recommend adding to positions.
${value} — neutral. Analysts see no compelling reason to buy or sell at current levels.
${value} — analysts are bearish. A meaningful number recommend reducing exposure.
${value} — consensus is deeply negative. Analysts expect significant downside.
${value} — analyst consensus. Review individual ratings for nuance.

analyst_consensus.whyMatters: Analyst ratings are a crowd-sourced second opinion. They are not infallible and often run too optimistic because firms prefer not to publish Sell ratings. Take strong ratings seriously, but still do your own homework.
analyst_consensus.scoringImpact: Strong Buy increases the score. Hold or Neutral is neutral. Sell ratings subtract. This factor carries heavy weight in the sentiment pillar.
commonMistakes: Treating consensus as a guarantee — even strong consensus can be wrong during unexpected events.
Ignoring the coverage count — a Strong Buy from one analyst is far less meaningful than a consensus from twenty.
analyst_consensus.example: Stock XYZ has twelve analysts covering it: five rate Strong Buy, four rate Buy, two rate Hold, and one rates Sell. The consensus is highly positive and adds to the sentiment score.
