insider_status.label: Insider Activity
insider_status.oneLiner: Whether company executives and directors are buying or selling their own stock.
insider_status.what: Insiders — CEOs, CFOs, board members — know their company better than any outsider. When they buy shares with personal cash, they are voting with their wallet that the stock is undervalued. When multiple insiders sell heavily, it can indicate that trouble is ahead, although sales also happen for diversification and personal tax reasons.
insider_status.howCalculated: Tracks SEC Form 4 filings from company insiders to determine net buying versus selling over the trailing quarter.

bands.text: ${value} — insiders are BUYING. Executives are putting their own money into the stock, which is one of the strongest bullish confidence signals.
${value} — insiders are SELLING. Single sales can be routine (diversification, taxes). Multiple heavy sales together are a warning sign.
${value} — no recent insider activity. No explicit signal from the people inside the building.
${value} — insider activity status.

insider_status.whyMatters: Insiders have the deepest knowledge of their business. When they are willing to risk personal wealth on the stock, it signals genuine conviction.
insider_status.scoringImpact: Insider buying gives a positive boost. Heavy or coordinated insider selling is a negative. In extreme cases, this can override other signals.
commonMistakes: Assuming every sale is a red flag — executives routinely sell for life events unrelated to company outlook.
Missing the bigger picture — one CEO buying $50k means little if the stock is at an all-time high and the CFO sold $5m.
insider_status.example: Three of the four C-suite officers bought shares in the open market over the last three months. That pattern is labelled buying and contributes a positive insider signal.

short_interest_pct.label: Short Interest
short_interest_pct.oneLiner: The percentage of shares that investors have borrowed and sold, betting the stock will fall.
short_interest_pct.what: Short sellers borrow shares and immediately sell them, hoping to buy them back cheaper later. Short interest shows how many people are making that bearish bet. A high number means scepticism is widespread; a low number means almost nobody is betting against the stock.
short_interest_pct.howCalculated: Total shorted shares divided by freely tradable shares outstanding, expressed as a percentage.

bands.text: ${value}% — VERY HIGH short interest. A huge crowd is betting this stock falls. If positive news hits instead, a short squeeze can rocket the price higher in days.
${value}% — elevated short interest. Notable bearish sentiment. Could be trouble, or it could set up a squeeze opportunity if the stock rallies.
${value}% — moderate short interest. Some scepticism is normal and does not imply disaster.
${value}% — low short interest. Very few investors are betting against this stock, which is generally a positive sign.

short_interest_pct.whyMatters: High short interest is mixed news. It signals doubt, but it also creates a potential squeeze: if short sellers rush to cover (buy back shares), their buying alone can push prices sharply higher. Short interest alone is therefore not a buy or sell signal.
short_interest_pct.scoringImpact: Very high short interest (above 20%) is flagged as a dealbreaker because it signals serious scepticism about the company. Moderate levels are informational and do not move the score much.
commonMistakes: Buying a stock just because it is heavily shorted — the shorts might be right, and the stock can decline for fundamentals, not squeeze.
Ignoring the short ratio (days to cover) — high short interest with low days to cover is far less dangerous than the reverse.
short_interest_pct.example: A stock with 22% short interest has many bears betting against it. If it misses earnings and falls 5%, nothing special happens. If it beats earnings and rises 8%, short sellers may rush to cover, accelerating the rally.

short_ratio.label: Short Ratio (Days to Cover)
short_ratio.oneLiner: How many trading days of normal volume it would take for all short sellers to exit their positions.
short_ratio.what: Short sellers hope to buy back shares cheaper later. The short ratio — also called Days to Cover — measures how long that bet has been building. If a restaurant had a reservation waitlist of 50 parties and could only seat 5 per night, it would take ten nights to clear. In the same way, a high short ratio means short sellers are crowded and exit pressure would take many days to clear. This value is identical to Days to Cover — same number, two names.
short_ratio.howCalculated: Total shorted shares divided by average daily trading volume over a recent window.

bands.text: ${value} days — EXTREME days to cover. Short sellers are deeply crowded; any positive catalyst can cause a violent rush to cover.
${value} days — high days to cover. The short crowd is crowded and vulnerable to upward surprises.
${value} days — moderate days to cover. Short sellers could cover their positions in a few normal sessions if needed.
${value} days — low days to cover. Short positions are thin enough that covering would barely register on the tape.

short_ratio.whyMatters: Short interest tells you who is betting against the stock; days to cover tells you how trapped those bears are. High interest combined with high days to cover forms a classic squeeze setup. The squeeze itself is not a buy signal — it is a risk amplifier.
short_ratio.scoringImpact: Does not directly change the score. Cross-referenced with short interest to flag squeeze potential. High values combined with positive momentum generate a boost.
commonMistakes: Confusing days to cover with the probability of a squeeze — a high ratio only matters if there is a catalyst to trigger buying.
Treating high days to cover as inherently bullish — the shorts might be correct, and the stock can continue falling.
short_ratio.example: A stock with 18% short interest and 6.2 days to cover sits in the elevated / high band on both measures. If the company guides higher next quarter, short sellers may scramble to buy back shares, adding upward pressure.

institutional_ownership.label: Institutional Ownership
institutional_ownership.oneLiner: The percentage of a company's shares owned by mutual funds, pension funds, and hedge funds.
institutional_ownership.what: Think of institutions as the grown-ups at the table. These are professional investors who run extensive due diligence before buying. High ownership means the stock has passed scrutiny by teams of analysts and portfolio committees. Light ownership does not automatically mean something is wrong, but it does mean fewer experts have vetted the stock.
institutional_ownership.howCalculated: Aggregates quarterly 13F filings from large institutions to compute the percentage of outstanding shares they collectively hold.

bands.text: ${value}% — strong institutional confidence. Big-money players have sized in heavily, usually after deep research.
${value}% — moderate ownership. Respectable institutional interest but not an all-in bet.
${value}% — light institutional ownership. Few large funds have taken positions.
${value}% — minimal institutional ownership. Professionals largely avoid the stock, which can signal unresolved risk.

institutional_ownership.whyMatters: Institutions generally have better access to management, research budgets, and legal constraints that prevent reckless gambling. If they avoid a stock, that is worth noticing.
institutional_ownership.scoringImpact: High institutional ownership adds to the sentiment score. Very low ownership is a concern. This factor carries moderate weight in the sentiment pillar.
commonMistakes: Assuming high ownership is always good — if institutions decide to sell together, the stock can gap down with no supportive buyers.
Ignoring whether the shares are held long term or are just short-term trading inventory.
institutional_ownership.example: A small-cap biotech with 8% institutional ownership sits in the minimal band. That alone does not say the science is bad, but it does warn that the professional money crowd has not embraced the story yet.

target_upside_pct.label: Price Target Upside
target_upside_pct.oneLiner: How much analysts expect the stock to rise from its current price, expressed as a percentage.
target_upside_pct.what: Analysts model a company's future profits and then guess what the stock should be worth. The average of all their target prices, minus the current price, becomes the target upside. A 15% upside means the average analyst thinks the stock could climb 15% before it becomes fairly valued.
target_upside_pct.howCalculated: Average of all published price targets for the stock, compared to the current trading price.

bands.text: ${value}% — huge upside. Analysts see massive room to run, but such high targets often come with high uncertainty attached.
${value}% — meaningful upside. A reasonable gap between today's price and where analysts think it should go.
${value}% — slight upside. The stock is seen as modestly undervalued by the analyst community.
${value}% — slight downside risk. Analysts consider the stock a bit expensive at current levels.
${value}% — significant downside expected. Analysts broadly see the stock as overvalued with meaningful risk ahead.

target_upside_pct.whyMatters: Price targets are not promises, but they reflect a consensus view of fair value. A stock sitting far above consensus targets may be priced for perfection, leaving little room for error.
target_upside_pct.scoringImpact: Strong upside above 15% contributes positively. Downside is negative. The conviction factor is tempered by how many analysts cover the stock — wider coverage means the figure is more reliable.
commonMistakes: Treating price targets as guarantees — analysts routinely miss badly on both the upside and downside.
Ignoring that targets lag news — they are updated infrequently and may already be stale after an earnings report.
target_upside_pct.example: A stock at $85 has twelve analysts with an average target of $103. The 21% upside places it firmly in the meaningful band. If four more analysts downgrade after a miss, the average target may fall closer to $92, changing the signal.

volatility_regime.label: Volatility Regime
volatility_regime.oneLiner: A category describing how wildly the stock price moves from day to day.
volatility_regime.what: Volatility is the bumpiness of the road. In a low-volatility regime the stock glides along like a luxury sedan on a smooth highway. In an extreme regime it bounces like a dune buggy over rocks. This classification helps your strategy match the ride: calm roads need tight stops, rough roads need room to breathe.
volatility_regime.howCalculated: Based on Average True Range percentage relative to price and recent historical percentile bands.

bands.text: LOW volatility. Steady, predictable day-to-day moves with few shocks. Ideal for tight stop placement.
NORMAL volatility. Typical movement that most swing traders expect. The sweet spot for most strategies.
HIGH volatility. Expect wider swings. Higher potential reward comes with higher risk; wider stops and smaller positions are appropriate.
EXTREME volatility. Moves are unusual and violent. Treat this as either a rare opportunity or a dangerous environment; mandatory wider stops and reduced sizing.
${value} — volatility regime.

volatility_regime.whyMatters: Your risk parameters should match the stock's personality. Trading a high-volatility name with tight stops will stop you out constantly; trading a low-volatility name with wide stops wastes capital.
volatility_regime.scoringImpact: Normal volatility is ideal. Low is slightly positive for stability. High is a negative because it increases risk. Extreme is a dealbreaker unless other factors are exceptional.
commonMistakes: Using the same stop-loss width for all stocks regardless of volatility — a 2% stop on a volatile name is a noise stop that will never stick.
Chasing high-volatility stocks for excitement without adjusting position size to match the larger swings.
volatility_regime.example: A utility stock may live in the low-volatility regime, while a speculative biotech often sits in high or extreme. The same 1% position size on both delivers very different risk profiles.

suggested_stop_pct.label: Suggested Stop Loss
suggested_stop_pct.oneLiner: The recommended emergency-exit distance below your entry price.
suggested_stop_pct.what: A stop loss is a circuit breaker. If the stock falls to this level, the original trade idea is probably wrong and exiting limits further damage. It is calculated from recent volatility, not picked arbitrarily. Think of it as the floor beneath a bungee cord: it does not prevent the jump, it prevents an uncontrolled fall.
suggested_stop_pct.howCalculated: Driven by the stock's Average True Range (ATR) and the swing-parity stop formula that multiplies ATR by a factor aligned with the volatility regime.

bands.text: ${value}% stop. Wide stop indicates a very volatile stock. Make sure position size is small enough that this loss remains within your risk budget.
${value}% stop. Above-average stop distance. Acceptable for medium-volatility names; verify it is not inside normal daily noise.
${value}% stop. Standard swing-trade stop. Tight enough to protect capital, roomy enough to avoid whipsaw exits.
${value}% stop. Tight stop suggests low volatility or an aggressive risk setting. Confirm the level gives the trade room to breathe.

suggested_stop_pct.whyMatters: Stop losses are the single most important risk-management tool. Without them, a 10% loss can silently become a 50% loss. With them, any single bad trade costs a known, bounded amount.
suggested_stop_pct.scoringImpact: Not a scoring factor. This is a risk-management recommendation calculated from the stock's volatility, not an input to the quality score.
commonMistakes: Moving the stop further away just because you do not want to be wrong — the stop exists to protect you, not to validate your ego.
Setting stops at psychologically obvious levels like round numbers where algorithms and market makers can easily find them.
suggested_stop_pct.example: A stock with a 4.2% suggested stop can drop roughly that amount before the system exits the position. If you risk the full 1% portfolio rule on this trade, position sizing adjusts accordingly so that a stop-out stays within budget.

suggested_position_size_pct.label: Suggested Position Size
suggested_position_size_pct.oneLiner: The percentage of your total trading capital the platform recommends allocating to this single position.
suggested_position_size_pct.what: Professional traders do not go all-in on one stock. They size each bet so that even a losing trade cannot do serious damage to the account. Higher volatility names get smaller allocations; calmer names can carry more weight. Think of it like wearing a helmet: the rougher the ride, the more protection you need.
suggested_position_size_pct.howCalculated: Derived from the 1% risk rule: portfolio value multiplied by max-risk-per-trade, divided by the entry price minus the stop-loss price.

bands.text: ${value}% of portfolio. Very large single-name exposure. Review your diversification rules carefully.
${value}% of portfolio. Solid position for a high-conviction trade in a well-behaved stock.
${value}% of portfolio. Moderate weight that leaves room for multiple concurrent positions.
${value}% of portfolio. Conservative size — often because the stock is volatile or the stop is wide.

suggested_position_size_pct.whyMatters: Position sizing is how professionals avoid blowing up their accounts. Even the best traders are wrong roughly 40% of the time. Reasonable sizing keeps you in the game long enough for the edge to play out.
suggested_position_size_pct.scoringImpact: Not a scoring factor. This is a risk-management output that protects your capital rather than judging whether the trade itself is good.
commonMistakes: Scaling into a losing position because the stock is cheaper now — that doubles down on a thesis you no longer have evidence for.
Treating suggested size as a target to maximise — if you override up, you must accept proportionally larger drawdowns.
suggested_position_size_pct.example: With a $50,000 account and the 1% rule, the maximum loss you can take on any trade is $500. If your stop is 5% below entry, the platform suggests a position near 2% of portfolio because 2% times 5% loss equals the $500 budget.

max_risk_per_trade_pct.label: Max Risk Per Trade
max_risk_per_trade_pct.oneLiner: The largest percentage of your total portfolio you should allow any single trade to lose.
max_risk_per_trade_pct.what: This is the golden rule of risk management. Even the best traders are wrong often. If you risk 1% per trade, you would need one hundred consecutive losses to reach zero, which is practically impossible in a lifetime. If you risk 10% per trade, just ten straight losses wipes you out. The difference is the difference between surviving and quitting forever.
max_risk_per_trade_pct.howCalculated: A configurable risk parameter you set before trading. The platform then sizes positions so that a stop-hit loss equals this percentage of your total capital.

bands.text: ${value}% max risk. Professional-grade and conservative. A hundred straight losses is needed to reach zero, so survival is very likely.
${value}% max risk. Reasonable for experienced traders who can stomach slightly larger swings per trade.
${value}% max risk. Elevated risk. A string of five losses cuts roughly a quarter of capital — only appropriate for very high-conviction setups.
${value}% max risk. Very aggressive. Ten straight losses ends the account. Reserved for extremely rare, high-edge opportunities.
${value}% max risk. Highly aggressive sizing. A short losing streak can cause serious damage quickly.

max_risk_per_trade_pct.whyMatters: Risk of ruin is real and mathematically simple. The 1% rule is why professional traders survive decades while amateurs blow up in months. It is not about being timid — it is about being consistent enough to trade tomorrow.
max_risk_per_trade_pct.scoringImpact: Not a scoring factor. It is a risk-management parameter that controls position sizing, not a judgement of whether the trade itself is good.
commonMistakes: Raising risk because you feel 'due for a win' — markets do not care about your feelings or past results.
Trying to make back losses faster by doubling risk — that is the fastest route to a blown account.
max_risk_per_trade_pct.example: At 1% max risk per trade with a $100,000 account, each position is sized so that a stop-out costs exactly $1,000. Losing ten trades in a row costs $10,000 — painful, but not catastrophic. At 10%, those same ten losses cost $100,000.

total_return_pct.label: Total Return
total_return_pct.oneLiner: How much money the strategy made or lost over the test period, expressed as a percentage.
total_return_pct.what: Total Return measures the raw profit or loss from start to finish. A 50% return means an account grew from $10,000 to $15,000 before fees. It does not account for risk.
total_return_pct.whyMatters: Return is the most obvious number, but it is meaningless without context. A 30% return looks impressive until you learn the strategy had a 40% max drawdown.
total_return_pct.scoringImpact: Displayed for context only. Our scoring engine does not use raw return as a quality signal.
commonMistakes: Chasing the highest return you see — highest-return backtests are often overfitted to past noise.
Ignoring the path to that return — a 40% return that dips -30% halfway feels very different from a steady climb.
total_return_pct.example: Strategy A: +40% total return with a -22% max drawdown. Strategy B: +28% total return with a -8% max drawdown. Strategy B is actually better because the ride was smoother.

sharpe_ratio.label: Sharpe Ratio
sharpe_ratio.oneLiner: Return earned per unit of total risk taken — the classic grade on whether the ride was worth it.
sharpe_ratio.what: The Sharpe Ratio divides excess return by total volatility. It answers: for every unit of bumpiness, how much extra return did you get? A Sharpe of 1.0 means you earned 1% extra return for every 1% of volatility.
sharpe_ratio.whyMatters: Sharpe lets you compare strategies fairly. Higher Sharpe means smoother, more reliable profits.
sharpe_ratio.scoringImpact: Strategies with Sharpe above 1.0 receive a quality boost. Sharpe below 0.5 is flagged as weak. Sharpe above 2.0 triggers an overfit review because extreme values on small samples are usually data mining.
commonMistakes: Treating Sharpe above 2.0 as automatically great — on fewer than 100 trades, a Sharpe of 2.5 is likely just lucky, not skillful.
Using Sharpe alone — it penalizes upside volatility too, which can unfairly punish strategies with big wins.
sharpe_ratio.example: A strategy with 12% annual return and 10% volatility has Sharpe = 1.0. If that same return came with 18% volatility, Sharpe drops to 0.56.

bands.text: ${value} — weak. The strategy is taking a lot of risk for very little extra return.
${value} — acceptable. The strategy earns enough to justify its volatility. Usable, but not great.
${value} — good. Solid risk-adjusted returns. Many professional strategies target this range.
${value} — exceptional but verify. A Sharpe above 2.0 is rare in real trading. Check that you have enough trades (100+) to trust this number.

sortino_ratio.label: Sortino Ratio
sortino_ratio.oneLiner: Like Sharpe, except it only counts the scary downside volatility and ignores pleasant upside bumps.
sortino_ratio.what: The Sortino Ratio is a twist on Sharpe. Instead of dividing by all volatility, it divides only by downside volatility. Upside volatility is good and should not be punished.
sortino_ratio.whyMatters: Many strategies have occasional huge winning trades. Sharpe treats those big wins as risk. Sortino does not, so it is a fairer grade for strategies with asymmetric returns.
sortino_ratio.scoringImpact: Used as a cross-check on Sharpe. When Sortino is meaningfully higher than Sharpe, the strategy likely has positive skew — big wins.
commonMistakes: Assuming Sortino is always better than Sharpe — it is only more useful when returns are asymmetric.
Using Sortino to hide bad risk — a strategy with frequent small losses and one huge win can have a great Sortino but terrible day-to-day reliability.
sortino_ratio.example: Strategy X has many small losses and three 30% winning trades. Sharpe = 0.9, but Sortino = 1.6 because downside volatility was mild.

calmar_ratio.label: Calmar Ratio
calmar_ratio.oneLiner: Annual return divided by the worst drawdown — a harsh but practical stress test.
calmar_ratio.what: Calmar Ratio takes annualized return and divides it by maximum drawdown. It answers: how much profit did I make for every dollar of peak-to-trough pain? A Calmar of 2.0 means you earned 2x what you briefly lost at the worst point.
calmar_ratio.whyMatters: Drawdown is psychological. Low Calmar means the strategy underperforms relative to its worst drawdown.
calmar_ratio.scoringImpact: Calmar below 1.0 is flagged. Calmar above 2.0 is considered strong.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the time spent in drawdown — Calmar uses max drawdown depth, not duration.
Comparing Calmar across different time periods — a 6-month Calmar of 2.0 is not the same as a 5-year Calmar of 2.0.
calmar_ratio.example: A strategy returned 18% annualized with a 12% max drawdown. Calmar = 18 / 12 = 1.5. If drawdown had been 25%, Calmar drops to 0.72.

bands.text: ${value} — poor. The strategy did not earn enough to justify its worst drawdown.
${value} — acceptable. Return roughly keeps pace with the worst loss experienced.
${value} — good. Solid compensation for drawdown risk.
${value} — strong. The strategy delivered significant return relative to its worst peak-to-trough decline.

max_drawdown_pct.label: Max Drawdown
max_drawdown_pct.oneLiner: The largest peak-to-trough loss the strategy ever experienced — the worst losing streak in dollars.
max_drawdown_pct.what: Max Drawdown is the largest percentage drop from any peak to any subsequent trough in the equity curve. If the account grew to $12,000 then fell to $8,000 before recovering, the max drawdown is -33%.
max_drawdown_pct.whyMatters: Drawdown is where traders quit. A strategy with a 40% max drawdown requires immense discipline to hold through. Max drawdown is a test of your stomach, not just your math.
max_drawdown_pct.scoringImpact: Max drawdown is used to flag psychologically brutal strategies. A drawdown above 25% triggers a warning. Below 15% is considered robust.
commonMistakes: Treating the worst so far as the worst possible — future drawdowns can always be deeper than history shows.
Comparing drawdowns without measuring recovery time — a -20% drawdown that takes 6 months to recover is worse than a -25% drawdown that bounces in 8 weeks.
max_drawdown_pct.example: Two strategies both have 15% annual returns. Strategy A max drawdown: -10%. Strategy B max drawdown: -28%. Both made the same money, but Strategy A let you sleep at night.

bands.text: ${value} — robust. The worst loss was mild. Most traders can stick with a strategy through this level of pain.
${value} — moderate. A noticeable drawdown, but survivable with disciplined position sizing.
${value} — psychologically brutal. A drawdown this deep will tempt you to abandon the strategy right before it recovers.

win_rate.label: Win Rate
win_rate.oneLiner: The percentage of trades that finished profitable — but win rate alone can lie.
win_rate.what: Win Rate is the fraction of trades that made money. 55% means 55 out of 100 trades were winners. Win rate is only half the picture. You must also consider how much you win versus how much you lose.
win_rate.whyMatters: Many beginners chase high win rates, but trading is about expectancy — the average amount you make per trade. An 80% win rate strategy with tiny wins and huge losses can lose money.
win_rate.scoringImpact: Win rate is contextualized against reward-to-risk in the engine. A high win rate with poor risk-reward does not receive a quality boost.
commonMistakes: Chasing 80%+ win rate systems — these often use very wide stops and tiny targets, producing negative expectancy.
Ignoring the relationship between win rate and risk-reward — the only number that matters is expectancy.
win_rate.example: Strategy A: 80% win rate, average win = $1, average loss = $5. Expectancy = -$0.20 per trade. LOSING. Strategy B: 45% win rate, average win = $3, average loss = $1. Expectancy = +$0.80 per trade. WINNING. Strategy B is better despite the lower win rate.

bands.text: ${value} — low. The strategy wins less than 4 of every 10 trades. It can still be profitable only with very strong reward-to-risk.
${value} — below average. Winning fewer than half your trades is normal for trend-following strategies. Check the average win size versus average loss size.
${value} — decent. The strategy wins more than it loses, which feels comfortable. You can still lose money with this win rate if losses are too large.
${value} — high. Solid majority of trades are winners. This is a strong signal IF the average loss is controlled.
${value} — very high. An 80%+ win rate sounds amazing, but check the reward-to-risk ratio. If your average win is smaller than your average loss, this system may actually be losing money.

profit_factor.label: Profit Factor
profit_factor.oneLiner: Gross profits divided by gross losses — a direct efficiency grade for the strategy.
profit_factor.what: Profit Factor is total money won divided by total money lost. A Profit Factor of 1.5 means the strategy made $1.50 for every $1.00 it lost. Every number above 1.0 means the strategy is profitable in aggregate.
profit_factor.whyMatters: Profit Factor strips away timing and psychology. It answers the simplest question: did I make more than I lost?
profit_factor.scoringImpact: Profit Factor below 1.0 is a hard reject. 1.0-1.3 is marginal. 1.3-1.5 is caution. 1.5-2.0 is good. Above 2.0 on small samples triggers an overfit warning.
commonMistakes: Trusting a Profit Factor of 3.0 from 20 trades — that is almost certainly curve-fit to past data.
Ignoring the sample size — Profit Factor from 30 trades can flip dramatically with 30 more trades.
profit_factor.example: Strategy X: 40 trades, gross profit = $4,200, gross loss = $2,800. Profit Factor = 1.5. Solid. Strategy Y: 25 trades, gross profit = $1,500, gross loss = $400. Profit Factor = 3.75. Impressive, but with only 25 trades, this could easily regress.

bands.text: ${value} — losing. The strategy lost more money than it made. Not usable as-is.
${value} — marginal. The strategy is barely profitable. It may survive in good markets but is vulnerable to changing conditions.
${value} — caution. The strategy is profitable, but the margin is thin. Monitor closely.
${value} — good. Solid efficiency. For every dollar lost, the strategy made between $1.50 and $2.00.
${value} — suspect overfitting. Profit Factors above 2.0 are rare in real trading. On fewer than 100 trades this is usually a sign the strategy memorized past noise.

expectancy.label: Expectancy
expectancy.oneLiner: The average profit or loss you can expect from one trade — the most important backtest number.
expectancy.what: Expectancy is calculated as: (win rate x average win) minus (loss rate x average loss). It tells you the expected value of a single trade before you take it. Positive expectancy means the strategy will make money over time.
expectancy.whyMatters: Expectancy combines win rate, average win, and average loss into one number. It is the only metric that definitively answers whether this strategy will make money if you follow it 100 times.
expectancy.scoringImpact: Expectancy is the primary quality filter in our engine. Positive expectancy is required. Higher expectancy means higher quality score.
commonMistakes: Using win rate alone to judge a strategy — an 80% win rate with tiny wins and huge losses has negative expectancy.
Expecting every trade to match the expectancy — individual trades vary wildly. Expectancy only holds over many trades (100+).
expectancy.example: A strategy with 45% win rate, average win = $200, average loss = $130. Expectancy = (0.45 x $200) - (0.55 x $130) = +$18.50 per trade. After 200 trades, you expect to earn about $3,700 — even though you lose 55% of the time.

bands.text: ${value} — no edge. On average, each trade is expected to lose money. This strategy will bleed capital over time.
${value} — marginal edge. The strategy is profitable, but barely. A small change in market conditions could erase it.
${value} — decent edge. The strategy earns enough per trade to justify execution costs and slippage.
${value} — strong edge. Each trade has a meaningful positive expectation. This is what professional systematic traders seek.

sqn.label: SQN (System Quality Number)
sqn.oneLiner: Expectancy adjusted for how consistent the results are — Van Tharp's compact strategy grade.
sqn.what: SQN combines three things: expectancy per trade, the variability of trade results, and the number of trades. Higher SQN means a larger edge relative to the noise.
sqn.whyMatters: A strategy with high expectancy but wildly bouncing results is harder to follow than one with moderate expectancy and steady results. SQN rewards both edge and consistency.
sqn.scoringImpact: SQN above 1.5 is adequate. SQN above 2.0 is good. SQN above 3.0 is excellent. Below 1.0 suggests the edge is small relative to variability.
commonMistakes: Using SQN on fewer than 30 trades — the number needs a reasonable sample to stabilize.
Confusing SQN with Sharpe — SQN focuses on per-trade expectancy; Sharpe focuses on return per unit of volatility.
sqn.example: Two strategies both have $25 expectancy per trade. Strategy A has SQN = 4.2 (consistent results). Strategy B has SQN = 1.3 (results bounce around wildly). Strategy A is much easier to trade psychologically.

ulcer_index.label: Ulcer Index
ulcer_index.oneLiner: Measures the depth and duration of drawdowns — how sick the equity curve made you feel.
ulcer_index.what: The Ulcer Index was created by Peter Martin in 1989. Unlike Max Drawdown, which only measures the deepest single drop, the Ulcer Index captures both how deep declines were and how long they lasted. It is the root-mean-square of all drawdowns from peak to trough.
ulcer_index.whyMatters: Max drawdown might say your worst loss was 25%. But if that loss took 4 months to recover, the psychological damage was worse than the number suggests. The Ulcer Index captures that cumulative pain.
ulcer_index.scoringImpact: Used alongside Max Drawdown to flag strategies that look acceptable on depth alone but cause lengthy underwater periods.
commonMistakes: Comparing Ulcer Index across different timeframes — longer backtests naturally accumulate more drawdown time.
Ignoring recovery speed — a strategy with Ulcer Index of 8 that recovers in 2 weeks feels very different from one with Ulcer Index of 8 that grinds for 5 months.
ulcer_index.example: Strategy A had a single -25% drawdown over 2 months. Strategy B had repeated -10% to -18% drawdowns that took 3-6 months to recover each time. Max drawdown favored A, but the Ulcer Index favored A much more strongly because the pain was concentrated and shorter.

entry_zone.label: Entry Zone
entry_zone.oneLiner: A price range where you want to buy, not a single exact number.
entry_zone.what: An entry zone is a band of prices where the stock looks attractive. Markets move fast, so chasing a precise entry rarely works. A zone gives you patience and flexibility.
entry_zone.example: A stock at $50 might have an entry zone of $48 to $49.50. You place a limit order somewhere in that range. If it never reaches your zone, you wait instead of chasing.

scale_in.label: Scale In
scale_in.oneLiner: Buying in pieces instead of all at once to reduce timing risk.
scale_in.what: Scaling in means splitting your intended position into multiple buys at different prices. If the stock drops, you pay a lower average price. If it jumps, you still have a partial position rather than missing the entire move.
scale_in.example: You want a $10,000 position. Buy 6% ($600) at the first signal, 3.6% ($360) if it dips 2% further, and 2.4% ($240) if it drops another 3%. Total: $12,000 invested with a better average price if the dip materialized.

r_multiple.label: R-Multiple
r_multiple.oneLiner: The core unit of trade math — every gain or loss measured against your initial risk.
r_multiple.what: R stands for the initial risk per share. If you buy at $50 and set a stop at $48, your R is $2 per share. A 2R target means you aim to make $4 per share — twice your risk. Every trade outcome is reported as an R-multiple: plus 2R, minus 1R, plus 0.5R.
r_multiple.whyMatters: R-multiple makes every trade comparable regardless of dollar size. A $500 profit on one trade and a $200 profit on another are meaningless without context. If the first risked $1,000 and the second risked $50, the second was actually the better trade.
r_multiple.example: Trade 1: Risked $2 per share, made $6. Result: plus 3R. Trade 2: Risked $5 per share, made $3. Result: plus 0.6R. Trade 1 was superior even though the dollar profit was smaller.

scale_out.label: Scale Out
scale_out.oneLiner: Taking partial profits at multiple targets instead of exiting the entire position at once.
scale_out.what: Scaling out means you sell portions of your position at different profit levels. You lock in some wins while letting the remainder run. It balances greed and fear.
scale_out.example: Buy 100 shares. Sell 40 shares at 1R profit, sell another 30 at 1.5R, sell the final 30 at 2R. At 1R, you move your stop on the remaining shares to breakeven so the rest of the trade is risk-free.

trailing_stop.label: Trailing Stop
trailing_stop.oneLiner: A stop loss that follows the price up — but never moves down.
trailing_stop.what: A trailing stop starts at your original exit level. As the stock price rises, the stop rises with it, usually by a fixed percentage or by recent swing lows. The critical rule: the stop never moves back down once raised.
trailing_stop.example: You buy at $50 with a 10% trailing stop ($45). The stock climbs to $60. Your stop is now $54. It drops to $55 — you are still in. If it drops to $53, the stop triggers and you exit with a $3-per-share win.

breakeven_move.label: Breakeven Move
breakeven_move.oneLiner: Raising your stop to your entry price after the trade moves in your favor.
breakeven_move.what: Once the stock has moved far enough in your favor, you move your stop loss to your original buy price. From that point, the worst outcome is neither a win nor a loss — you break even. It turns a risky trade into a risk-free one.
breakeven_move.example: You buy at $50 with a stop at $48. The stock rises to $52, a 2R gain. You move your stop to $50. Now if the stock drops back to $50, you exit with zero profit and zero loss. You cannot lose money on this trade anymore.

time_stop.label: Time Stop
time_stop.oneLiner: Exiting a trade after N days if it has not moved — dead money has a cost.
time_stop.what: A time stop says: if this trade has not acted within X days, sell regardless of whether you are up or down. Capital sitting in a flat stock is capital that is not working for you elsewhere.
time_stop.example: You set a 10-day time stop. The stock sits at $51 for 10 days after you bought at $50. You sell at $51 for a tiny win, freeing capital to deploy into a stock that is actually moving.

risk_limits.label: Risk Limits
risk_limits.oneLiner: Hard rules that cap exposure — your personal circuit breakers.
risk_limits.what: Risk limits are non-negotiable boundaries. Maximum position size as a percent of your account. Maximum percentage of your portfolio in one sector. Maximum allowed loss in a single day. They keep you alive during drawdowns.
risk_limits.example: Rules: never hold more than 5% of capital in one stock, never risk more than 1% of capital on a single trade, stop trading for the day after a 2% portfolio loss. These rules prevent one bad day from becoming a blown account.

technical.title: Technical Analysis
technical.whatItIs: Technical analysis studies the stock's PRICE and VOLUME data to gauge direction and momentum. It does not care about the company's products or profits — it only looks at what the market is DOING.
technical.whyItMatters: A stock's price eventually follows its earnings: technical analysis does not care about the company's products or profits — it only looks at what the market is DOING.
technical.howScoreWorks: We look at 7 factors: MA alignment (trend direction), RSI (momentum), ADX (trend strength), ATR (volatility), Volume Ratio (interest), Bollinger Band position, and MACD (momentum signal). Each factor is scored, then combined into a -1.0 to +1.0 score. The trend alignment and RSI get the most weight.

fundamental.title: Fundamental Analysis
fundamental.whatItIs: Fundamental analysis looks at the COMPANY's financial health: how much money it makes, how fast it's growing, how much debt it has. It answers: is this a good business?
fundamental.whyItMatters: A stock's price eventually follows its earnings. Good fundamentals do not guarantee the stock will go up tomorrow, but they strongly predict where it'll be in 1-3 years. Technical plus fundamental together give you the complete picture.
fundamental.howScoreWorks: We score 11 factors: market cap (size), P/E (valuation), EPS (profitability), profit margin (efficiency), debt/equity (financial risk), revenue growth (expansion), free cash flow yield (cash generation), dividend yield (shareholder returns), return on equity (capital efficiency), price-to-book (asset valuation), and operating margin (core business efficiency). Positive values mean good. Negative values mean concerning. The final score combines these into -1.0 to +1.0.

earnings.title: Earnings Analysis
earnings.whatItIs: Companies report their financial results every 3 months (quarterly earnings). This analysis looks at their track record of beating or missing expectations, and when the next report is due.
earnings.whyItMatters: Earnings reports cause the biggest single-day moves in stock prices (5-20% is common). Knowing the earnings track record helps you assess whether the company consistently delivers or frequently disappoints.
earnings.howScoreWorks: We look at the latest surprise percentage, the beat rate (how many of the last 4 reports beat expectations), and the average stock reaction to earnings. Consistent beaters get positive scores. Consistent missers get negative scores.

sentiment.title: Market Sentiment
sentiment.whatItIs: Sentiment measures what OTHER market participants think about the stock: professional analysts, company insiders, and short sellers. It is like getting a consensus opinion from everyone watching the stock.
sentiment.whyItMatters: When everyone is bullish, the stock usually goes up — until it does not. When insiders are buying heavily, it is one of the most reliable signals. When short interest is extreme, be careful.
sentiment.howScoreWorks: We combine: analyst consensus (weighted heavily), insider buying/selling activity, institutional ownership percentage, short interest and days to cover, price target upside potential, and beta (how much the stock moves relative to the market). The overall range is -1.0 to +1.0.

risk.title: Risk Assessment
risk.whatItIs: Risk analysis tells you how DANGEROUS this trade is and how to manage that danger. It is not about predicting direction — it is about protecting your money.
risk.whyItMatters: Even the best analysis can be wrong. Risk management separates professionals from amateurs. Professionals focus on how MUCH they can lose. Amateurs only think about how MUCH they can make.
risk.howScoreWorks: We assess volatility (ATR percentage), calculate an appropriate stop loss level, determine the right position size based on volatility, and suggest how much of your portfolio to risk. The score ranges from -1.0 (extreme risk) to +1.0 (very safe).

sector_rotation.label: Sector Rotation
sector_rotation.oneLiner: Which industries lead or lag changes over time as money flows between sectors.
sector_rotation.what: Sector rotation shows which industries are leading and lagging. Leading sectors tend to continue outperforming for a period. Think of it like fashion trends — what is in style changes over time as investors move money between sectors.
sector_rotation.example: When tech is leading and utilities are lagging, investors are in a risk-on mood. When utilities lead and tech lags, they are in a risk-off mood.

risk_on.label: Risk-On vs Risk-Off
risk_on.oneLiner: Investor mood swings between optimistic buying and scared selling.
risk_on.what: Risk-on means investors are optimistic and buying growth stocks, tech, and smaller companies. Risk-off means they are scared and buying safer assets like utilities, bonds, and gold.
risk_on.example: Risk-on: Bitcoin rallies, tech stocks surge. Risk-off: Gold rises, utilities outperform.

conviction_score.label: Conviction Score
conviction_score.oneLiner: How confident the system is in a trade idea, from 1 to 10.
conviction_score.what: The conviction score measures how strongly multiple independent signals agree. Seven or higher means several unrelated checks aligned. Four to six means mixed evidence. One to three means weak or conflicting signals.
conviction_score.example: A stock at conviction 8 out of 10 means technical, fundamental, and sentiment all agree on the direction — rare and more reliable than a stock at conviction 3.

regime.label: Market Regime
regime.oneLiner: The current personality of the broad market — trending, choppy, or volatile.
regime.what: Market regime describes whether the market is in a strong uptrend, a choppy sideways range, or a high-volatility environment. Different strategies work best in different regimes.
regime.example: In a strong-trend regime, momentum strategies shine. In a choppy ranging regime, mean-reversion strategies work better.

regime_states.label: Regime States
regime_states.oneLiner: The market’s current “weather” and its sub-conditions — the context that shifts how every score is weighted.
regime_states.what: Exuberance: euphoric buying, valuations stretched. Risk-On: steady gains with healthy participation; trend strategies shine. Neutral: no clear directional bias; stock-specific setups matter more than market calls. Cautious: sellers gaining ground; tighten stops and shrink positions. Risk-Off: broad selling; capital preservation first. Crisis: panic conditions; cash is a position. Sub-conditions refine these: defensive_flight (investors rushing to safety), risk_on (high confidence), choppy (no clear direction with frequent reversals), strong_trend, ranging, high_vol, low_vol. The regime re-weights scoring: trend counts most in strong trends; volume and quality lead in choppy markets.
regime_states.whyItMatters: The same setup behaves differently in different weather. A breakout in Risk-On is routine; the same breakout in Risk-Off usually fails.
regime_states.example: Score 53 (Neutral) means mixed signals — keep position sizes normal but demand extra confirmation before adding risk. Score 25 (Risk-Off) means the same stock gets a smaller position or a pass.

stop_loss.label: Stop Loss
stop_loss.oneLiner: An automatic exit order that limits your loss if the trade goes wrong.
stop_loss.what: A stop loss is your emergency exit. If the stock drops to a preset price, you sell automatically. It prevents a small loss from becoming a large one.
stop_loss.example: You buy at $100 and set a stop at $90. If the stock drops to $90, you sell and limit the loss to 10%. Without a stop, a -10% loss can turn into -50% if you hold and hope.

position_sizing.label: Position Sizing
position_sizing.oneLiner: How much of your money goes into each trade — the most important risk control.
position_sizing.what: Position sizing decides the percentage of your portfolio to allocate to a single trade. The goal is that no single loss should hurt your account significantly. One to two percent risk per trade is standard for professionals.
position_sizing.example: With a $100,000 account risking 1.5% per trade, the maximum loss on any single position is $1,500.

diversification.label: Diversification
diversification.oneLiner: Spreading your money across different investments to reduce risk.
diversification.what: Do not put all your eggs in one basket. Diversification spreads your capital across sectors, asset classes, or strategies so that one bad position does not sink your account.
diversification.example: Instead of buying 5 tech stocks, buy 1 tech plus 1 healthcare plus 1 energy plus 1 finance plus 1 consumer. If tech crashes, the others may hold steady.

pre_market.label: Pre-Market Trading
pre_market.oneLiner: Trading that happens before the regular market session opens.
pre_market.what: Pre-market prices show where a stock trades before the market opens, typically 4:00 AM to 9:30 AM Eastern. Big pre-market moves often set the tone for the day.
pre_market.example: If a stock gapped up 3% pre-market after strong earnings, expect a higher opening price. A -3% pre-market drop suggests something disappointed.

verdict.label: Verdict
verdict.oneLiner: The system's overall opinion: Strong Buy, Buy, Watch, Hold, Avoid, or Sell.
verdict.what: The verdict is the final summary of all the analysis. It combines module scores, conviction, and dealbreakers into one action.
verdict.example: Strong Buy means exceptional setup with high conviction and aligned signals. Avoid means significant problems were found across multiple checks.

graduation.label: Graduation Path
graduation.oneLiner: Professional Mode unlocks features gradually over 90 days to avoid overwhelm.
graduation.what: Instead of dumping every tool on new users at once, the platform progressively unlocks deeper analysis. Start with basics like the Morning Brief and Verdict, then gain access to advanced screens, deep analysis, and trade-plan tools.
graduation.example: Day 1: Morning Brief plus Verdict. Day 14: All 21 screener columns. Day 30: Deep analysis tabs and trade-plan tools.

var.label: Value at Risk (VaR)
var.oneLiner: The maximum loss you can expect over a given time period, with a set confidence level.
var.what: VaR answers: how bad could things get? A 1-day 95% VaR of $500 means there is a 5% chance you lose more than $500 in one day. It is a worst-case snapshot, not a guarantee.
var.example: A $50,000 portfolio with a 1-day 95% VaR of $1,200 means on 19 out of 20 normal days, losses stay under $1,200. The 1-in-20 day could be worse.

cvar.label: CVaR (Conditional Value at Risk)
cvar.oneLiner: The average loss in the worst-case tail beyond VaR — how bad things get when they go wrong.
cvar.what: CVaR, also called Expected Shortfall, goes beyond VaR. If VaR says you might lose $1,200, CVaR asks: if you are in the losing 5%, what is the AVERAGE loss? CVaR is usually larger than VaR and considered a more complete risk measure.
cvar.example: Portfolio VaR (95%) = $1,200. CVaR (95%) = $2,100. When the bad day happens, the average loss is $2,100, not just $1,200.

kelly_criterion.label: Kelly Criterion
kelly_criterion.oneLiner: A formula for sizing bets so your wealth grows fastest over time without ruin.
kelly_criterion.what: The Kelly Criterion calculates the mathematically optimal position size based on your win rate and the typical win versus loss. It tells you the percentage of capital to risk on each bet to maximize long-term growth.
kelly_criterion.example: If your strategy wins 55% of the time and your average win is $1.10 per $1 risked, Kelly suggests risking about 10% of capital per trade. Most traders use half Kelly (5%) to reduce volatility.

correlation_matrix.label: Correlation Matrix
correlation_matrix.oneLiner: A grid showing how strongly different holdings move together — from lockstep to opposite.
correlation_matrix.what: A correlation matrix compares every pair of assets in a portfolio. A correlation of +1 means they move together perfectly. A correlation of -1 means they move in opposite directions. Zero means no relationship.
correlation_matrix.example: A portfolio of 5 tech stocks might show correlations of +0.7 to +0.9. That is barely diversified. Add utilities (correlation near 0) or bonds (negative correlation during some periods) and the portfolio becomes safer.

liquidity.label: Liquidity
liquidity.oneLiner: How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price.
liquidity.what: Liquidity is the width of the market for a stock — how many willing buyers and sellers exist right now. Think of a farmers' market vs a rare collectibles auction: at the market you can trade anytime at fair prices; at the auction, one sale can swing the price wildly. Volume and spread are its vital signs.

glossary.definition: Expecting the price to go up. Named after a bull lifting upward with its horns.
Expecting the price to go down. Named after a bear swiping downward with its paws.
How much and how quickly a stock's price moves up and down. High volatility means big swings. Low volatility means steady prices.
The speed and strength of a price move. A stock with strong momentum keeps moving in the same direction.
The general direction a stock moves over time. An uptrend makes higher highs. A downtrend makes lower lows. Sideways means no clear direction.
When a stock's price moves above a resistance level or below a support level. Often signals the start of a new trend.
A temporary dip in an uptrend. The price drops a bit but the overall upward direction remains. Often a good buying opportunity.
Betting that a stock will go down. You borrow shares, sell them, and hope to buy them back cheaper later.
When a heavily shorted stock rises instead of falling, forcing short sellers to buy back shares quickly, which pushes the price even higher.
The average price over a set number of days. It smooths out daily noise to show the underlying trend direction.
How easy it is to buy or sell a stock without moving the price. High liquidity means many buyers and sellers.
How much an investment falls from its peak. A 20% drawdown means the account is down 20% from its highest value.
How much you could gain compared to how much you could lose on a trade. A 3:1 ratio means you could make $3 for every $1 you risk.
Deciding how much money to put into a single trade. The goal is to limit any single loss to a small percent of your total portfolio.
Spreading your money across different stocks to reduce risk. If one stock crashes, others may be fine.
Every trade result measured against your initial risk per share. A 2R win means you made twice your risk. A -1R means you lost exactly your risk.
Buying a position in multiple pieces instead of all at once. Reduces the average cost if the price dips after your first buy.
Selling portions of a position at different profit targets instead of exiting everything at once.
A stop loss that rises with the stock price but never falls. It locks in profits as the stock climbs.
A stop loss placed at a technical level such as a recent swing low or support zone, not at an arbitrary percentage.
Raising a stop loss to the entry price after the trade moves in your favor. From that point, the worst outcome is neither profit nor loss.
An exit rule based on time, not price. If a trade has not moved after N days, you sell to free up capital.
A price range where a stock looks attractive to buy, giving you flexibility instead of requiring an exact price.
An automatic sell order placed below your entry to limit losses. The single most important risk management tool.
An automatic sell order placed at your target price to lock in gains. Usually set at a multiple of your risk.
When multiple unrelated signals point in the same direction. Confluence increases confidence because independent checks rarely all mislead at once.
A 1-10 score measuring how strongly independent signals agree. High conviction means many checks aligned; low conviction means mixed or conflicting evidence.
A critical issue that overrides otherwise positive signals. Examples: extreme short interest, low volume, or negative fundamental drift.
A warning sign that something is wrong with a setup. Multiple red flags usually mean the trade is not worth taking.
The market's current personality: strong uptrend, choppy range, or high volatility. Strategies perform differently in each regime.
How a stock performs compared to the broader market or its sector. A stock with high relative strength is outperforming its peers.
Volume-Weighted Average Price. The average price weighted by trading volume. Institutions often compare executions to VWAP.
Exponential Moving Average. A moving average that gives more weight to recent prices, reacting faster than a simple moving average.
Simple Moving Average. The average price over a set number of days. Slower to change than an EMA but smoother and less jumpy.
When a short-term moving average crosses above a long-term moving average. Historically bullish, often preceding major advances.
When a short-term moving average crosses below a long-term moving average. Historically bearish, often preceding major declines.
The number of shares actually available for trading. Companies with low float can move sharply on modest buying or selling pressure.
The percentage of shares that have been sold short. High short interest means many investors are betting the stock will fall.
How many days of average trading volume it would take for all short sellers to buy back their shares. Higher numbers mean more squeeze potential.
Average True Range. A measure of how much a stock typically moves each day. Used to set stop losses and position sizes.
Average Directional Index. Measures trend strength from 0 to 100. Below 20 means weak or no trend. Above 25 suggests a developing trend. Above 50 means a strong trend.
The difference between a fast and a slow exponential moving average. It shows whether short-term momentum is strengthening or weakening.
A smoothed version of the MACD line, usually an EMA of the MACD itself. Crossovers between MACD and Signal generate buy or sell signals.
The visual gap between the MACD line and the Signal line. It shrinks before crossovers and grows after, giving an early sense of momentum shifts.
When Bollinger Bands narrow tightly. Low volatility often precedes high volatility — a squeeze can signal an impending breakout.
The average profit or loss expected from one trade. Formula: (win rate times average win) minus (loss rate times average loss). Positive expectancy means an edge.
Gross profits divided by gross losses. Above 1.0 means the strategy made more than it lost. Higher is better, but extreme values need large sample sizes.
Return earned per unit of total volatility. It compares strategies by measuring reward for every unit of risk taken.
Like Sharpe, but it only counts downside volatility. Upside volatility is treated as good and ignored, making Sortino more forgiving for strategies with big wins.
Annualized return divided by maximum drawdown. It asks whether the return was worth the worst peak-to-trough loss experienced.
System Quality Number. A Van Tharp metric combining expectancy, variability, and trade count into a single strategy grade.
Measures the depth and duration of drawdowns. Lower is better. It captures cumulative pain better than max drawdown alone.
The percentage of trades that finish profitable. Win rate alone is misleading without the reward-to-risk ratio.
Value at Risk. An estimate of the maximum loss possible over a set time with a given confidence level. A 95% one-day VaR of $500 means a 5% chance of losing more than $500.
Conditional Value at Risk. The average loss in the worst tail beyond VaR. Also called Expected Shortfall. It answers what happens when the bad scenario actually occurs.
A formula for the mathematically optimal bet size based on win rate and average win versus average loss. Most traders use half Kelly for safety.
A measure of how two assets move together. Plus 1 means lockstep. Minus 1 means opposite directions. Zero means no relationship.
How much a stock moves compared to the overall market. Beta of 1 means in line. Above 1 means amplified moves. Below 1 means muted moves.
Companies with market capitalization typically above $10 billion. Established, generally more stable, and slower growing than smaller companies.
Companies with market capitalization roughly between $2 billion and $10 billion. More growth potential than large-cap but with more risk.
Companies with market capitalization under $2 billion. Higher growth potential but also higher risk, lower liquidity, and more volatility.
Price-to-Earnings ratio. How much investors pay per dollar of company profit. High P/E can signal growth expectations or overvaluation.
Earnings Per Share. The company's profit divided by its number of shares. Growing EPS over time is a sign of a healthy, growing business.
Cash a company generates after paying for all operations and capital expenses. Free cash flow shows how much real cash the business produces.
Return on Equity. How efficiently the company uses shareholder money to generate profit. Higher ROE suggests a strong competitive advantage.
Price-to-Book ratio. Compares the stock price to the company's accounting book value. Useful for valuing asset-heavy businesses like banks.
P/E divided by earnings growth rate. It adjusts valuation by growth. A PEG near 1 suggests fair value; below 1 may signal undervaluation.
Total debt divided by shareholder equity. High ratios mean more financial risk. Low or negative ratios mean conservative balance sheets.
Short-term assets divided by short-term liabilities. It measures whether the company can pay its near-term bills. Below 1.0 is a warning sign.
Revenue left after core business costs, before interest and taxes. It shows how profitable the fundamental business is, separate from financing decisions.
A price level where buying interest has historically been strong enough to stop a decline. Think of it as a price floor.
A price level where selling pressure has historically prevented further gains. Think of it as a price ceiling.
The difference between the bid price and the ask price. Tight spreads mean lower trading costs. Wide spreads can signal low liquidity.
The difference between your expected fill price and the actual execution price. More common in volatile or low-liquidity markets.
How many times over a company could pay its interest expenses from operating profit (EBIT ÷ interest). Below 2x means profit barely covers debt costs — risky if earnings dip.
The share of earnings paid to shareholders as dividends (dividends ÷ net income). A 50% payout leaves half the profit to reinvest; above ~80% is hard to sustain.
Like the current ratio but excludes inventory — can the company pay its next 12 months of bills with truly liquid assets? Above 1.0 is healthy; below 0.7 warrants caution.
The gap between the highest price buyers offer and the lowest price sellers accept. Wide spreads are an invisible tax on every trade — common in low-volume stocks. Also just called "the spread".

The overall personality of the market right now — trending up, chopping sideways, or swinging wildly. The best setups differ in each regime, so the first question an elite trader asks is: what kind of market am I in?
A market mood where capital flows freely into stocks and other risky assets. Prices tend to rise and momentum setups work well. The opposite of Risk-Off.
A defensive market mood where investors flee risky assets and hoard cash or bonds. Prices fall, rallies fade, and you want smaller size and wider stops. The opposite of Risk-On.
A frothy, greed-driven phase where buyers chase strength and pullbacks barely happen. Legitimate but dangerous — late entries catch the reversal, so the plan (stop + target) matters even more.
A fear-driven phase of heavy selling and wild volatility. Most systems tighten or stand aside; if you trade, size is tiny and stops are non-negotiable.

A range-bound market with no strong trend. In a neutral regime, fade-the-extremes and breakout-from-range setups often beat chasing momentum; respect the two boundaries instead of betting on a breakout.
